5. **Hollywood studios as an underutilized video training data source:** Goldberg raises an original argument that Hollywood and television studios possess enormous quantities of high-quality, physics-accurate, multi-angle visual data — including footage that never made it into final productions — that could be transformative for training video AI models. He suggests that whoever secures access to studio video libraries could gain a significant training data advantage, and the host half-jokingly suggests Elon should acquire movie studios for this purpose.

6. **Elon's three-part AI strategy:** The host summarizes Elon's competitive position as: (1) owning the world's largest supercomputers and building more faster, (2) dramatically compressing training cycles to weeks rather than months, and (3) possessing unique real-world vision data from Tesla vehicles that no other AI lab can access. He argues it is more likely Elon can acquire the general training data he is currently missing than it is for competitors to replicate Tesla's proprietary vision dataset.

Notable quotes and data:
- Grok 4.2 runs on 500 billion (0.5 trillion) parameters and is "missing important training data" — Elon Musk's own admission
- Colossus 2 is training 7 simultaneous models: Imagine v2, two 1T variants, two 1.5T variants, one 6T model, one 10T model
- 1 trillion parameter Grok model expected in ~2–3 weeks; 1.5 trillion parameter model in ~4–5 weeks
- Pre-training timelines: current large models ~2 months; newer 1T–1.5T models ~2–5 weeks
- Grok 5 expected to be based on a 6 trillion and 10 trillion parameter model
- Anthropic's Sonnet described as roughly 2x the size of Grok; Opus described as roughly 10x the size
- "The AI in FSD is far beyond the frontier. It is the frontier for all of the others. No questions about that." — Larry Goldberg
- "Robotaxi shouldn't be confused with this conversation" — Goldberg, emphasizing FSD/robotaxi readiness is independent of the general AI race
- "We're not even in the beginning — we're just at the beginning of the beginning of seeing the new stack emerge." — Larry Goldberg
- Tesla's AI described as two-layer: FSD = system one (reactive), Grok = system two (reasoning)
- Cortex 2 described as expected to be completed in "a couple of years" for Optimus brain training

articles.title: BREAKING: Tesla Launches FSD in Europe!
articles.body:
This video is a live breaking news stream covering the formal approval of FSD Supervised in the Netherlands by the RDW (Dutch Vehicle Authority), marking the first official FSD approval in continental Europe. Host Herbert is joined by Jeff Lutz and Amsterdam-based Tesla enthusiast and advocate Kees Roolvink Schapendonk, who helped lobby for the approval and was celebrating at midnight when the news broke. The core argument is that the Netherlands approval is a historic domino that could trigger rapid mutual recognition across all 27+ EU member states, dramatically expanding Tesla's FSD market.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Supervised formally approved in the Netherlands by the RDW:** Tesla Europe announced that FSD Supervised has received formal regulatory approval from the RDW (the Dutch type approval authority) and will begin rolling out in the Netherlands shortly. The RDW's official statement emphasized that "due to the continuous strict monitoring of the driver in the vehicle, the system is safer than other driver assistance systems," and noted they had "thoroughly researched and checked the system for more than a year and a half." The approval was granted under an exemptionary article that allows regulators to fast-track novel technology not yet captured by existing regulatory frameworks.

2. **Netherlands approval as a gateway for EU-wide rollout:** Because the RDW is the governing type approval body in Europe — every vehicle with an E4 stamp from the RDW is approved Europe-wide — the Netherlands approval creates a mutual recognition pathway for all other EU member states. Tesla itself cited a summer 2026 timeline for broader EU rollout, with Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, Austria, and the Nordics expected to follow. A fast-track timeline of 4 to 8 weeks for some countries was discussed, with medium and slower tracks also possible depending on national discretionary authority.

3. **Regulatory significance — EU and UNECE must now respond:** Kees explained that the exemption granted to Tesla by the RDW places Tesla's FSD above the existing regulatory framework, meaning both the EU (European Commission) and the UNECE (United Nations Economic Commission for Europe) are now compelled to respond and update their own regulations to accommodate the technology. This was characterized as a "big baller move" by Tesla, effectively forcing supranational regulatory bodies to follow suit.

4. **Current global FSD Supervised approval footprint:** As of the video, FSD Supervised is approved in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Puerto Rico, Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, and now the Netherlands. Supervised trials are already launched in Abu Dhabi as of March 1, 2026. A partial approval for China has occurred, with a full approval anticipated soon based on signals in the software. Israel's transport minister has publicly stated FSD approval is coming soon, and Japan is also expected to follow.

5. **FSD version used in Netherlands testing and approval:** Kees noted that during Tesla's final ride-along session the Friday before approval, he observed a version change from prior weeks and spotted on-screen notifications never seen in US versions, which he believes were specific RDW requirements added during the testing period. He suggested Europe will receive a slightly adjusted version of what is available in the US but still very similar. Jeff Lutz noted that the 14.2 series has been "really stable" in the US for several months. An FSD version referenced as 14.3 was mentioned as being even more responsive, though the regulatory testing was conducted on older versions.

6. **Tesla's multi-year EU testing program:** Kees noted that Tesla has been testing FSD in approximately seven to nine European countries over the past two years, covering varying road conditions, signage differences, and merging behaviors across countries like France, Germany, Spain, and Italy. He reported that FSD performed consistently across these countries, with road harmonization since the 1950s making European driving environments more similar than different.

7. **Legacy OEM contrast:** Kees drew a pointed contrast between legacy automakers who loudly promised full autonomy by 2025 back in 2019–2020 and have since repeatedly retracted those claims, versus Tesla, which he credited as "the only company that followed through and stayed persistent on their goal." He gave particular credit to Tesla's policy team for grinding through years of regulatory resistance.

8. **Border-crossing notification feature:** Kees noted that Tesla added an in-vehicle on-screen notification that alerts drivers when they are about to cross a national border within Europe, warning that FSD Supervised functionality might deteriorate. He attributed this feature to the ongoing patchwork of national approvals and said it will likely remain in place for some time as other countries work through their own approval processes.

9. **Estimated Tesla fleet in Europe eligible for FSD:** Jeff Lutz estimated approximately 1.2 million Teslas sold in Europe since 2020, potentially rising to 1.5 million if going back further — representing the installed base that could immediately access FSD Supervised as the rollout expands across EU member states.

## Market & Competition

1. **European regulatory lobbying by legacy OEMs:** Kees stated that legacy OEMs were actively lobbying against FSD approval in Europe back in 2019–2020, vocally opposing Tesla's push for regulatory acceptance while simultaneously making their own unfulfilled autonomy promises. This lobbying is credited as a significant reason why the European regulatory process was so slow and contentious.

Notable quotes and data:
- RDW statement: "Due to the continuous strict monitoring of the driver in the vehicle, the system is safer than other driver assistance systems. We have thoroughly researched and checked the system more than a year and a half."
- Tesla Europe announcement: "Trained on billions of kilometers of real-world driving data, it can drive you almost anywhere under your supervision from residential roads to city streets and highways. No other vehicle can do this."
- Tesla cited summer 2026 for broader EU mutual recognition rollout.
- Fast-track timeline for other EU countries: 4 to 8 weeks estimated.
- Approximately 27 EU member states eligible for mutual recognition following Netherlands approval.
- Kees paid 7,500 euros out of pocket to be among the first FSD subscribers in the Netherlands.
- Kees drove approximately 30,000 miles across 33 US states over 2 months, with roughly 95% of driving on FSD.
- Abu Dhabi supervised FSD trials launched March 1, 2026.
- FSD versions referenced: v13, v14, 14.2, and 14.3.

articles.title: The FSD Release Note Nobody Is Talking About
articles.body:
This episode of the cernbasher channel features a deep-dive conversation between the host and Phil on the significance of the FSD 14.3 release notes, particularly two technical changes that the broader community has largely overlooked: a major shift toward reinforcement learning and a ground-up rewrite of the AI compiler and runtime using MLIR. The discussion expands into broader themes including the convergence of Tesla and SpaceX into a distributed compute-and-intelligence fabric, the trajectory of Optimus development, and a bold prediction that unsupervised robotaxi operations in Austin are imminent — possibly by end of April 2026.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3's two underappreciated breakthroughs:** Phil identifies two major technical changes in FSD 14.3 that he considers more significant than the widely discussed 10x parameter count claim. First, Tesla has dramatically deepened its use of reinforcement learning (RL) to address edge cases surfaced during supervised robotaxi testing in Austin and the Bay Area. Rather than fixing individual intersection problems, RL allows Tesla to categorically cure classes of suboptimal driving behavior by defining ideal trajectories, scoring alternatives from poor to near-ideal, and reinforcing the desired behavior during training on AI4 hardware in the Cortex data center in Texas. Second, Tesla rewrote its AI compiler and runtime from the ground up using MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation), an open-standard framework that abstracts model operations from hardware while enabling aggressive optimization of both compute and memory efficiency. The release notes explicitly state this resulted in a 20% faster reaction time and improved model iteration speed.

2. **Why the 10x parameter claim may be overstated or misunderstood:** Phil argues that the widely anticipated 10x increase in parameter count from the previous version may not have materialized as described, or may be irrelevant to what 14.3 actually delivers. He explains that a 10x parameter model run on AI4 hardware would likely drop inference throughput from the required 36 cycles per second to something closer to 12, making it non-viable for real-time vehicle control. He speculates that the team may have prototyped such a model, confirmed it couldn't run efficiently on HW4, and pivoted to RL as the more effective mechanism for eliminating the long tail of edge cases. He notes Elon's public statements often reflect aspirational roadmap items that shift during engineering review cycles and should not be taken as hard commitments to any specific version.

3. **Hardware tier implications for unsupervised FSD:** Phil draws a clear line between hardware generations and their unsupervised FSD potential. He states with high confidence that Hardware 3 vehicles will likely achieve a reasonable level of supervised FSD but will never support unsupervised operation. Hardware 4 is expected to support unsupervised robotaxi operation with high confidence, and unsupervised customer-owned vehicle operation with slightly less certainty. AI5 hardware is seen as providing substantial headroom — estimated between 2x and 10x — to run significantly larger models and is expected to enable robust unsupervised FSD across all use cases.

4. **FSD unsupervised and robotaxi are essentially the same neural network problem:** Phil clarifies that at the neural network layer, unsupervised customer FSD and unsupervised robotaxi are approximately 90% the same problem. The distinction is mostly product-level rather than model-level. He estimates that roughly 90% of the current engineering focus is on robotaxi deployment, with the remaining 10% on consumer unsupervised FSD, even though advancing one effectively advances the other.

## Robotaxi

1. **Unsupervised robotaxi in Austin predicted as imminent:** The host made a public prediction that unsupervised robotaxi operations would launch in Austin by end of April 2026. While acknowledging the prediction is intentionally provocative and not made with 100% confidence, he cites multiple converging signals: FSD 14.3 appears to be the version that has been running in Austin in build-candidate form for approximately two to three months; the release reflects months of real-world RL refinement from supervised robotaxi observer feedback; and Cybercabs are now being spotted and tested across multiple cities including San Antonio, Dallas, Phoenix, and Miami, which he interprets as calibration and pre-deployment preparation ahead of dropping the safety observer in Austin.

2. **Cybercab sightings and fleet calibration underway:** Joe Tegtmeyer spotted and counted approximately 60 Cybercabs in various locations, some appearing in groupings. Phil explains these are engineering test vehicles that retain steering wheels and pedals. Some have been observed with solid-state LiDAR units mounted on top, which Phil believes are being used for calibration purposes — specifically to map the slightly different camera placements on the Cybercab body relative to Model Y, Model 3, and other vehicles. Tesla's neural network includes an abstraction layer for camera geometry, but physical calibration of production-intent vehicles across multiple cities is a prerequisite to scaling the fleet.

3. **Supervised vs. unsupervised observer positioning by city:** Phil notes a regulatory distinction between Austin and the Bay Area. In Austin, safety observers sit in the passenger seat, while Bay Area regulations require them to be in the driver's seat. The spread of Cybercab testing to multiple new cities is interpreted as a signal that Tesla is close to pulling the safety observer from the Austin fleet entirely and committing to fully unsupervised operation there.

4. **Waymo safety and experience comparison:** Phil briefly acknowledges that Waymo has a reasonably good safety record but argues its rider experience has been poor — citing incidents of vehicles blocking roads and passengers being temporarily unable to exit. He argues Tesla is deliberately moving slowly on removing safety oversight because it takes both safety and ride experience seriously, and that this caution is appropriate even if frustrating to observers who want faster deployment.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus V3 teased via shrouded design image:** The host references what appears to be a preview or conceptual image of Optimus V3, described as a shrouded or fabric-covered humanoid form. Phil interprets Elon's approach as wanting to present the closest achievable humanoid form factor for V3, with the fabric covering serving a functional purpose of protecting exposed actuator joints from debris and mechanical interference. He draws a parallel to Apple's product reveal strategy — noting that Apple did not preview the iPhone before launch — and suggests Elon's early reveals are strategic for talent recruitment, investor awareness, and competitive signaling rather than purely technical readiness.

2. **Manufacturing scale as Optimus's defining constraint:** Phil argues the hardest part of the Optimus program is not the AI stack or actuator capability but manufacturability at scale. He references Tesla's stated goal of building a factory capable of producing 10 million Optimus units annually as a starting point, describing this as an extraordinarily capital-intensive and logistically complex undertaking. He contends Elon is willing to let competitors make mistakes and learn from them, because his confidence lies in Tesla's vertical integration advantage and manufacturing know-how — the same thesis he applies to Cybercab.

3. **Power and compute constraints are Optimus's central engineering challenge:** Phil estimates Optimus carries approximately 2 to 2.5 kilowatt-hours of battery capacity, while its AI chip (currently AI5, eventually AI6) can consume up to 250 watts. Combined with actuator power demands for physical movement, the power budget creates a severe constraint. He predicts the final months of the Optimus engineering program will be dominated by engineers optimizing the compute-to-battery trade-off, potentially offloading intelligence tasks to external compute nodes via network rather than running them on-device.

4. **Optimus deployment path — factory first, consumer later:** Both hosts agree that the most economically rational deployment path begins in warehouse and manufacturing environments, where even a robot that can only move boxes provides high economic value across multiple shifts, before transitioning to service industry roles and eventually consumer home use. However, Phil notes that if AGI is the objective, training across diverse home and public environments will be necessary, not just structured factory settings. The AI stack for Optimus is described as a superset of the FSD vision stack, with the addition of a language/reasoning layer and physical skill decomposition — the ability to break complex tasks like making an omelette into constituent sub-skills.

5. **Optimus on the moon and Mars:** Phil discusses Elon's post suggesting off-Earth deployment of Optimus will proceed faster and at greater scale than on Earth. He frames manufacturing on the moon or Mars using Optimus as a potential path to vastly cheaper products through lower-cost robotic labor in resource-rich environments. He acknowledges significant engineering challenges remain — including temperature variance, lunar dust, and gravity differences requiring design adjustments — but argues Optimus-class robots will be the dominant life form in those environments once present.

## Market & Competition

1. **XAI Colossus 2 scaling and frontier model competition:** Phil discusses Elon's post that XAI's Colossus 2 facility now has seven models in simultaneous training, including Grok 4.2 at half a trillion parameters and two variants of a one-trillion parameter model, with a six-trillion parameter model also referenced. Phil explains this reflects Elon's strategy of parallelizing model development to accelerate learning — running multiple architectural variants simultaneously, identifying the strongest performer, and discarding the rest. He frames this as Elon attempting to leapfrog Anthropic and OpenAI on frontier model capability, while acknowledging Google remains a more difficult target in the West.

2. **Vision AI and the Optimus connection to XAI's imaging work:** Phil connects Elon's continued investment in image generation (referred to as "Imagine") to Optimus development, arguing that vision input and output capabilities are prerequisites for AGI and directly feed the Optimus visual stack. He dismisses the interpretation that image generation is frivolous consumer entertainment, framing it instead as foundational research for embodied AI.

3. **Distributed intelligence routing as an emerging infrastructure challenge:** The host proposes a concept he calls an "intelligence routing layer" — analogous to how the internet routes data or power grids route electricity — that would optimize in real time which compute nodes handle which AI tasks, based on cost, availability, latency, and capability specialization. Phil discusses this as an open problem, noting that today's agentic AI frameworks like Grok 4.2 route sub-tasks internally within a single vendor's infrastructure but do not yet route across competing providers. He draws an analogy to TCP/IP as a potential standard that could emerge, and speculatively connects Tesla's Autobidder (used for Megapack energy arbitrage) as a possible architectural precursor to such a routing system.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD 14.3 release note: *"Rewrote the AI compiler and runtime from the ground up with MLIR resulting in 20% faster reaction time and improve model iteration speed."*
- Phil on Hardware 3: *"Hardware 3 may end up with a reasonable supervised FSD but will never go unsupervised."*
- Phil on Hardware 4: *"Hardware 4 will most certainly be unsupervised for robotaxi, slightly less clear for unsupervised for you and I."*
- Phil on AI5: *"AI5 — they've got somewhere between 2x to 10x the headroom to be able to run this stuff."*
- On the 10x parameter claim: *"Elon always speaks in orders of magnitude so that's kind of his natural numeric nomenclature."*
- On the inference requirement: *"They require the data to run through those inference cycles 36 times a second."*
- On Optimus's battery: *"You've got a relatively small battery, maybe 2.5 kilowatt hours of energy on Optimus."*
- On Optimus AI chip power: *"That thing's running at 250 watts."*
- On Optimus factory target: *"It's building a factory to build 10 million of these things on an annualized production basis as a starting point."*
- On the robotaxi prediction: *"I think it's imminent now."* (as of April 8, 2026)
- Joe Tegtmeyer counted approximately 60 Cybercabs spotted in various locations.
- Grok 4.2 described as a half-trillion parameter model; one-trillion parameter variants currently in training at Colossus 2; six-trillion parameter model also mentioned.
- Previous FSD version prior to 14.3 referenced as version 14.2.25, believed released approximately December 2025.

articles.title: The New Luddities of AI
articles.body:
This video from farzad-fm draws a historical parallel between the 19th-century Luddite movement and the 2026 AI data center moratorium bill introduced by Senator Bernie Sanders and co-sponsored by Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. The host's core thesis is that attempts to stop transformative technologies through legislation have never succeeded historically — they only relocate the technology elsewhere — but that the political pressure such movements generate can still produce meaningful worker protections. The video is primarily a historical, political, and economic essay rather than a Tesla- or EV-specific analysis, though the host briefly mentions being heavily invested in Tesla and AI companies.

## Market & Competition

1. **The Sanders-AOC AI Data Center Moratorium Act:** On March 25th, 2026, Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the AI Data Center Moratorium Act, co-sponsored in the House by Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. The bill does not regulate how AI is used, does not create worker retraining programs, and does not impose taxes on automation — instead, it bans the construction of new AI data center buildings. The host argues this is equivalent to trying to stop the automobile by banning roads, and that the technology would simply relocate to countries without such restrictions.

2. **Sanders' Broader Policy Proposals:** Beyond the moratorium, Sanders has proposed a "robot tax" on companies that replace workers with automated systems, a 32-hour work week with no reduction in pay, 20% worker ownership of stock in large corporations, and 45% of corporate board seats allocated to employees. Sanders' office released a report in October 2025 claiming approximately 100 million U.S. jobs — roughly two out of three jobs in the American economy — are at risk from AI. The host distinguishes these broader proposals as legitimate subjects for debate, unlike the moratorium itself.

3. **Global AI Competition and the Relocation Argument:** The host argues that a U.S. moratorium would not slow AI development by even a single day, as China is investing hundreds of billions of dollars in AI through 2030 and has made AI dominance a national priority. The UAE has launched a national AI strategy and is building large data center campuses, Singapore is offering tax incentives and fast-track permits to position itself as Southeast Asia's AI hub, and even El Salvador is courting AI companies with zero-tax incentives. The host contends that restricting U.S. data center construction would simply shift AI model training to Shenzhen or Abu Dhabi instead of Virginia or Texas.

4. **Historical Pattern of Technology Suppression:** The host walks through four historical examples where restrictions on transformative technologies backfired. England's Red Flag Act of 1865 required a person to walk ahead of automobiles with a red flag, limited speeds to 2 mph in towns, and was not fully lifted until 1896 — by which time France had captured nearly 50% of the global automobile market and Britain lost its lead in the automobile revolution. American farmers' anti-automobile legislation in rural communities was similarly futile; within 25 years, farmers became the most enthusiastic adopters of cars and tractors. The U.S. halt on nuclear plant construction after Three Mile Island in 1979 resulted in over 100 reactor cancellations, and by 2026 the U.S. is scrambling to restart nuclear capacity for AI data center power — with Microsoft signing a deal to restart the actual Three Mile Island plant. The EU's restrictions on GMO crops led to productivity disadvantages relative to the U.S., Brazil, and Argentina, and the EU became dependent on importing the very GMO crops it had banned.

5. **Energy Costs and Wealth Concentration as Real Concerns:** The host acknowledges that the concerns motivating the bill are legitimate. A typical large AI data center consumes around 100 megawatts of electricity — equivalent to powering approximately 80,000 homes — and in some communities these facilities are genuinely driving up electricity prices for residents. The Trump administration has reportedly asked hyperscalers to subsidize additional power costs so electricity prices do not increase for local residents. The host also acknowledges that AI benefits are flowing disproportionately to those who already own capital, noting his own AI expenditure is approximately $2,000 per month and yields significant productivity gains that most people cannot replicate.

6. **Labor Economics Data on Automation Displacement:** The host cites MIT economists Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo, who published data showing that between 1947 and 1987, automation displacement and reinstatement of new jobs were roughly balanced — displacement destroyed approximately 0.48% of labor demand per year while new tasks created approximately 0.47% per year. Since 1987, however, displacement accelerated to approximately 0.7% per year while reinstatement slowed to approximately 0.35% per year, producing a compounding gap that adds up to roughly a 10% net reduction in labor demand over 30 years. Research also found that each additional industrial robot per 1,000 workers reduced the employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 to 0.34 percentage points. Acemoglu, who won the Nobel Prize in economics, stated in 2024 that AI is being used "too much for automation and not enough for providing expertise and information to workers," and estimates only about 5% of human tasks will be fully replaced by AI over the next decade.

7. **The Luddite Legacy and What Comes After Failed Bills:** The host argues that the original Luddites were not technophobes but highly skilled workers — stocking frame knitters, croppers, and shearers — who had exhausted every legal avenue before resorting to machine-breaking because trade unions had been made illegal under the Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800. Their unrest contributed to the repeal of those acts in 1824, legalizing trade unions for the first time. This led to the Factory Act of 1833 (banning child labor under age 9 in textile mills, limiting children aged 9-13 to 8-hour days, and establishing government inspectors), and the Ten Hours Act of 1847. The host's conclusion is that the Sanders-AOC moratorium will fail to pass — given that too many states want data center jobs and tax revenue — but that the political pressure it generates may produce meaningful downstream policy such as worker retraining funds, data center energy offset requirements, or tech company taxes funding transition support.

Notable quotes and data:
- Sanders' October 2025 report claims ~100 million U.S. jobs are at risk from AI, roughly two out of three jobs in the American economy.
- AOC, on March 27th, 2026 (two days after the bill was introduced), pledged that politicians should refuse money from AI companies.
- A typical large AI data center consumes ~100 megawatts of electricity, equivalent to powering ~80,000 homes.
- Microsoft signed a deal to restart the Three Mile Island nuclear plant to power AI data centers.
- Acemoglu (2024): "My argument is that we currently have the wrong direction for AI. We're using it too much for automation and not enough for providing expertise and information to workers."
- Post-1987 labor data: displacement ~0.7% per year vs. reinstatement ~0.35% per year — a gap that compounds to roughly a 10% net reduction in labor demand over 30 years.
- Each additional industrial robot per 1,000 workers reduced the employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 to 0.34 percentage points.
- Acemoglu estimates only ~5% of human tasks will be fully replaced by AI over the next decade.
- England's Red Flag Act (1865–1896): 31 years of restrictions; by the time they were lifted, France held ~50% of the global automobile market.
- The host's personal AI spend: ~$2,000/month, with described "massive boosts in efficiency."
- The British government deployed 12,000 soldiers against Luddite workers; 17 Luddites were executed by hanging, dozens more deported to Australian penal colonies.

articles.title: Has Tesla Lost Its Way?
articles.body:
This video from the "futureaza" channel is part of a recurring series titled "Are They Doomed?" in which host Brian evaluates Tesla across several dimensions — engineering culture, demand, cost controls, cash on hand, and roadmap — to argue that despite growing skepticism and competitive pressure, Tesla is not doomed. The core thesis is that Tesla's pivot away from being purely a car company toward autonomous transportation-as-a-service, energy storage, Optimus, and chip manufacturing gives it a roadmap that competitors cannot easily match. Brian scores Tesla across categories and arrives at an overall score of 74 out of a possible higher total, which he describes as the best score in the series so far.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Declining Global Delivery Trend:** Brian presents Tesla's global delivery figures showing a peak of approximately 1.8 million vehicles followed by two consecutive years of declining deliveries. He acknowledges this trend is "not great for demand" and notes that Giga Berlin and Giga Texas both carry surplus capacity they are not fully utilizing. He scores Tesla's demand a six out of ten — "better than average, not great" — while noting this could improve as FSD matures and robotaxi deployment begins.

2. **Cybertruck Economics Under Scrutiny:** Brian flags the Cybertruck as a cost outlier relative to its sales volumes, stating that its costs are "out of line" for the number of units being sold. However, he frames the Cybertruck as a necessary engineering stepping stone — used to validate Tesla's 48-volt architecture, steer-by-wire system, and other technologies that feed directly into the Cybercab platform. He stops short of calling it a success but sees strategic justification for its development.

3. **FSD as a Demand Catalyst:** Brian argues that Full Self-Driving is a meaningful differentiator that drives purchase intent in markets where it is available, with some U.S. customers unwilling to buy a car without that capability. He qualifies this by noting that in many countries FSD is not available, making Tesla "just a car" in those markets — a position where competitive pressure from companies like BYD is more acute.

## Market & Competition

1. **BYD Surpasses Tesla in Global BEV Sales:** Brian briefly acknowledges that BYD has officially surpassed Tesla in global battery electric vehicle sales, referencing what appears to be a mid-2025 article. He downplays the significance of this milestone, noting that BYD has its own challenges and that surpassing Tesla in unit sales does not mean Tesla is finished, particularly given Tesla's pivot toward services and software.

2. **Competitive Moat in Robotaxi Economics:** Brian argues that neither Uber, Waymo, Lyft, nor any other competitor can match the cost structure Tesla is building for its robotaxi network, particularly through the Cybercab's design decisions. He frames this as a structural, engineering-driven advantage rather than a temporary lead.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD as a Global Expansion Opportunity:** Brian discusses FSD's current limitations — particularly its unavailability in many international markets — as a factor suppressing demand today but representing significant upside as regulatory approvals expand. He frames unsupervised FSD as the unlock for a new category of demand, including from buyers who currently would not purchase a non-autonomous vehicle.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi Is Inevitable Regardless of Belief:** Brian makes a conviction argument that the robotaxi transition is coming whether or not skeptics accept it, comparing disbelief in it to disbelief in gravity. He frames the Cybercab's engineering and cost structure as uniquely advantaged, and states that no competitor can match Tesla on price once the network is deployed at scale.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Described as a Near-Ready but Deliberately Held Product:** Brian suggests that Optimus could be sold today in its current form and would find buyers, but Tesla is choosing to wait — letting "the soufflé rise a bit" before release. He raises the question of how many units Tesla plans to sell versus retain for internal use as robots-as-a-service, noting that a keep-heavy strategy would require significant upfront capital that would weigh on the balance sheet.

## Energy

1. **Megapack Deployments Accelerating:** Brian highlights a GitHub tracker maintained by a community member that catalogs global Megapack installations, describing the deployment pace as fast and growing. He characterizes each Megapack unit as generating hundreds of thousands of dollars in profit and notes that the energy storage segment is already revenue-positive on an ongoing basis. He calls this part of the roadmap "very exciting."

## Financials

1. **$44.1 Billion Cash on Hand — Impressive for a Car Company, Insufficient for Tesla's Ambitions:** Brian reports Tesla holds $44.1 billion in cash, which he describes as exceptional by automotive industry standards but potentially insufficient given the capital requirements of Optimus deployment, robotaxi fleet buildout, and the Terafab chip manufacturing facility. He scores cash on hand a six out of ten for this reason.

2. **Terafab Cost Estimates Range Widely — Up to $50 Billion and Beyond:** Brian discusses the Terafab chip fabrication facility (co-funded with SpaceX) and notes that while an early estimate pegged costs at $20–25 billion (described as a low estimate), a Barclays report puts the figure at $50 billion, with some other estimates going even higher. He acknowledges uncertainty about whether the project will ultimately succeed, noting that Tesla has canceled major initiatives before (including Dojo and battery swap).

3. **Cost Controls Scored Highly:** Brian scores Tesla's cost controls an eight out of ten, citing vertical integration (in-house battery production, in-house lithium refining, in-house seat manufacturing), a lean model lineup strategy, direct-to-consumer sales eliminating dealership markups, and a culture of continuous cost reduction. He draws a historical parallel to Henry Ford's Model T, which ran for nearly 20 years while its price dropped from approximately $2,500 to $5–600.

4. **Engineering Culture Scored Eight Out of Ten:** Brian scores Tesla's engineering culture an eight, drawing on personal conversations with Tesla engineers who described a culture where feedback is not just accepted but demanded. He contrasts this with traditional automakers where minor engineering changes can take months or years, and where siloed hierarchies prevent open communication.

5. **Overall Roadmap Score of Nine Out of Ten:** Brian awards Tesla's roadmap a nine out of ten — the highest category score — citing the Cybercab, Optimus, Megapack, and the Terafab as key pillars. The deduction from a perfect score reflects uncertainty around Terafab costs and unresolved complications in its development. Tesla's composite score across all categories reaches 74, which Brian describes as the highest in the series.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla cash on hand: **$44.1 billion**
- Terafab cost estimates: **$20–25 billion** (low estimate), **$50 billion** (Barclays estimate), with some projections described as far higher
- SpaceX is reportedly paying **half** of the Terafab bill
- Global Tesla deliveries peaked at approximately **1.8 million** before declining two consecutive years
- Model T price range cited: started at ~**$2,500**, ended at ~**$5–600** over nearly **20 years** of production
- Engineering score: **8/10** | Demand score: **6/10** | Cost controls: **8/10** | Cash on hand: **6/10** | Roadmap: **9/10** | Composite: **74**
- Dojo was canceled; battery swap was also canceled — cited as evidence Tesla is willing to exit initiatives that don't pan out
- "Megapack represents hundreds of thousands of dollars in profit for every single unit"
- "There isn't a single front on which Uber or Waymo or Lyft or any of the others can compete on price [with Tesla's robotaxi]"

articles.title: Terafab a GO, FSD Update, and a whole lot more - Tesla Beat Podcast
articles.body:
This episode of the Tesla Beat Podcast (episode 141) covers a wide range of Tesla-related topics including the latest FSD v14.3 update, Cybercab production observations, the Tesla/Intel chip foundry partnership, Tesla Semi competitive positioning, and global EV market dynamics. The hosts — joined by Brian, Matthew, and Joe — frame Tesla's near-term moves around autonomous driving and robotaxi deployment as the central thesis, while providing color on competitive pressures facing legacy automakers and the broader EV trucking market.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD v14.3 rollout impressions:** The hosts report that FSD v14.3 has rolled out and features a completely rebuilt AI compiler, resulting in approximately 20% faster reaction times. The host notes personal testing in San Jose, including narrow roads and school drop-offs, and observes that the system feels more assertive and confident compared to prior v14 releases, particularly in parking decisions — the system now targets the first available spot rather than circling repeatedly.

2. **Remaining v14.3 issues — navigation regressions:** Despite improvements, navigation remains a known regression across v14 sub-releases. Hosts report the system routing to incorrect destinations (e.g., loading docks, wrong addresses) and not consistently showing parking pin indicators across all location types. One host notes workarounds like entering a neighbor's address to prevent the system from targeting an incorrect driveway approach.

3. **FSD architecture context — small vs. large model:** Elon Musk is quoted as saying the small model has advanced so fast that the large model has not yet caught up. V15 is identified as the large model update, suggesting the current v14.x line represents small model iterations and that more substantial capability jumps are expected with V15.

4. **Training data milestone approaching 10 billion miles:** Tesla is reportedly close to 9.2 billion miles of FSD training data, with Sawyer Merritt cited as the source. Elon Musk has said roughly 10 billion miles is needed to achieve unsupervised self-driving. The host notes the accumulation rate is approximately 1,000 miles every 4 seconds. The hosts caution that Elon used the word "roughly," meaning hitting 10 billion may not be a hard trigger for unsupervised deployment.

5. **Netherlands FSD regulatory approval imminent:** FSD regulatory approval in the Netherlands is described as potentially imminent, with posts suggesting it could happen very soon. The hosts note that once approved in the Netherlands, other EU countries could accept that approval without requiring individual country-level testing and approval processes, potentially unlocking FSD across Europe quickly.

6. **Unsupervised robotaxi operation in Austin already functionally ready:** The hosts assert that Tesla already has the software capable of unsupervised robotaxi operation running in Austin, noting that supervisors in Austin are no longer actively at the controls. The remaining blockers are described as regulatory and internal readiness thresholds, not technical capability.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab production ramp visible at Fremont:** The host reports personally observing approximately 60 Cybercabs in two groups in the Fremont outbound lot. Crash testing is underway and vehicles are being shipped across the United States for environmental testing in different conditions. Trailers at the Fremont factory are being used to bring Cybercabs in and out after testing runs on the factory track.

2. **Cybercab seen as imminent, not vaporware:** Brian pushes back on skeptics, arguing that manufacturers do not produce hundreds of units for something speculative. The pattern of nationwide shipping for testing, combined with Austin supervisors no longer actively controlling vehicles, signals that commercial deployment is on the near-term roadmap, likely starting in Austin.

3. **S and X factory winding down for robotaxi/Optimus transition:** The hosts note that custom Model S and X orders have been closed, prices on remaining inventory have been raised approximately $15,000, and the Fremont line is winding down SNX production. This is framed as Tesla clearing the runway for the Cybercab and Optimus production ramp using the unboxed manufacturing method.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **SNX factory conversion underway:** The hosts connect the end of Model S/X production to Tesla's stated plans to repurpose that factory space for Optimus production. The unboxed manufacturing method and the conversion of the SNX line are described as clear signals that Tesla is serious about Optimus at scale. No specific Optimus production numbers or timeline dates are stated.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Model Y dominates China March sales:** Joe presents March China sales data showing the Model Y at approximately 39,000 units, with the next closest competitor at roughly 31,000 units — a gap of approximately 25%. Brian contextualizes this as remarkable given Tesla's limited model lineup versus Chinese competitors offering 10–30 vehicles.

2. **Tesla outsold BYD in Q1 for total EV volume:** The hosts note that Tesla outsold BYD across all models in Q1 2026, which is described as a significant feat given BYD's broader market presence, more factory capacity, and lower price points. Brian cautions this lead is unlikely to hold long-term.

3. **New Model Y (YL) expanding globally:** The refreshed long-wheelbase Model Y is expanding to multiple new markets. Israel is cited specifically, with first deliveries starting in June. The model has also expanded to nine or ten additional markets across Asia. Brian notes that Tesla marketing the YL under the Model Y name mirrors Toyota's Corolla strategy — using a single popular nameplate to aggregate sales across distinct variants.

4. **Giga Texas Model Y line reportedly down for two weeks:** Matthew mentions reports that the Model Y line at Giga Texas may be down for approximately two weeks, speculating this could be related to retooling for the long-wheelbase Model Y for the North American market.

5. **Model S and X price increases on remaining inventory:** Tesla raised prices on remaining Model S and X inventory by approximately $15,000, attributed to addition of a "Lux package." The hosts frame this as rational end-of-life inventory pricing, not a demand signal, comparing it to dealership markups on rare models.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla Semi competitively positioned as the only sub-$300K Class 8 electric truck:** Brian reports that Tesla Semi is priced between approximately $240,000–$260,000 based on California rebate application public records — roughly half the price of competing electric Class 8 trucks priced at $400,000–$500,000. He identifies $300,000 as the economic break-even threshold for fleet operators. With California rebates of $120,000–$150,000, the Semi becomes cheaper than diesel from day one.

2. **Electric trucking industry broadly struggling outside Tesla:** Brian describes the Daimler Freightliner eCascadia going from roughly 2% of line production to a "rounding error," while Matthew's contact at a competing truck manufacturer reports BEV order share among competitors dropping from ~10% to 0.5–1%, with his own company holding at 5–10%. The rollback of U.S. ZEV credits and emissions mandates is cited as the primary driver of the collapse in demand.

3. **Tesla Semi efficiency advantage:** Brian cites real-world trucker data showing Tesla Semi achieving approximately 2.1 kWh per mile, versus the industry standard of 1.7–1.8 kWh per mile for typical Class 8 electric trucks. A Canadian study comparing eCascadia to Cascadia found $167,000 CAD (~$140,000 USD) in savings over six years, but at $400,000–$500,000 purchase price, the payback period is too long for most operators.

4. **Tesla/Intel chip foundry partnership:** The hosts discuss a reported partnership between Tesla, SpaceX, and Intel to build a chip foundry in the U.S. Brian frames it as Tesla and SpaceX providing funding while Intel provides manufacturing expertise, potentially reducing what would have been a $100 billion, 10-year effort to approximately a $30 billion, five-year timeline. Intel is described as one of only three companies globally capable of producing chips to Tesla's required precision, alongside TSMC and Samsung.

5. **Toyota CEO warns of existential threat from Chinese EV competition:** The Toyota CEO is quoted as saying "Unless things change, we will not survive. I want everyone to acknowledge this sense of crisis." The hosts frame this as a recognition Japanese OEMs are arriving at far too late.

6. **BMW acknowledges software-defined vehicles:** BMW publicly stated that "cars are now defined by software, not engines." The hosts react skeptically, noting that acknowledging this reality means little without restructuring the fragmented multi-supplier software architecture that legacy OEMs rely on.

7. **Japan incentivizing locally sourced EV components:** Japan has introduced incentives favoring domestically produced and locally sourced vehicles, effectively disadvantaging BYD imports. Notably, Teslas (made in China) were still reportedly qualifying for top-tier incentives at the time of discussion.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD v14.3 AI compiler rebuilt from scratch → ~20% faster reaction times
- Tesla FSD training data at ~9.2 billion miles (Sawyer Merritt); Elon said "roughly 10 billion" is the target
- Training data accumulation rate: ~1,000 miles per 4 seconds
- Tesla Semi price range from California rebate records: approximately $240,000–$260,000
- California rebates on Tesla Semi: $120,000–$150,000, making it cheaper than diesel day one
- Tesla Semi real-world efficiency: ~2.1 kWh/mile vs. industry average 1.7–1.8 kWh/mile
- Canadian eCascadia vs. Cascadia study: ~$167,000 CAD savings over 6 years
- Tesla Semi reportedly 50% cheaper per mile to operate in California (per a Tesla/Semi spokesperson cited by host)
- Model Y China March sales: ~39,000 units; nearest competitor ~31,000 units (~25% gap)
- Tesla outsold BYD total EV volume in Q1 2026
- Intel partnership estimated to reduce chip foundry timeline from ~10 years/$100B to ~5 years/$30B
- ~60 Cybercabs observed in Fremont outbound lot in two groups
- Model S/X remaining inventory price increased ~$15,000 with Lux package addition
- Israel Model Y deliveries starting June 2026
- V15 identified as the large model FSD update; current v14.x is small model
- BEV order share at competing truck OEMs dropped from ~10% to ~0.5–1% following U.S. incentive rollbacks

articles.title: Will Tesla BUY Intel To BOOST Terafab?
articles.body:
This video from the channel "jobhakdi" — hosted by Jo Bhakdi — argues that Intel's announcement of joining Terafab is far more significant than it appears on the surface, framing it as a potential precursor to a Tesla acquisition of Intel. Jo Bhakdi contends that Tesla and SpaceX's long-term vision — building a Kardashev Type 2 civilization by deploying AI-inference satellites in space powered by free solar energy — creates an urgent need for massive domestic chip manufacturing capability, a gap Intel is uniquely positioned to fill. The core thesis is that Intel, despite being commercially weakened, is strategically the ideal acquisition target for Elon Musk's constellation of companies due to its American onshore status, vertically integrated fab capabilities, and relative vulnerability compared to rivals like Nvidia, TSMC, or Samsung.

## Market & Competition
1. **Intel joins Terafab — a signal of deeper strategic alignment:** Jo Bhakdi highlights that Intel has announced it is joining Terafab, a new initiative described on its website as designed to make humanity a "galactic civilization" built around the Kardashev scale. He argues this is not a minor partnership but a potential first step toward Intel being absorbed into the Tesla/SpaceX ecosystem. Intel is characterized as the "ugly duckling" of chip manufacturers — once dominant, now sidelined by Nvidia on AI chips and by AMD on CPUs — making it both capable and vulnerable enough to be an acquisition candidate.

2. **Why Intel is the right acquisition target and not the others:** Jo Bhakdi systematically rules out other chip companies as acquisition targets for Tesla: Nvidia is the world's largest company and not acquirable; TSMC is Taiwanese and subject to geopolitical risk from China; Samsung is a strategic national asset for South Korea; Broadcom is deeply tied to Tesla's competitors (Amazon, Google); and AMD is relatively too strong. Intel, by contrast, is an American company with a market cap of approximately $250 billion, struggling financially but still possessing significant engineering talent, brand value, and vertically integrated fab manufacturing know-how — making it, in Jo Bhakdi's view, the "perfect match."

3. **Tesla's current chip partnerships as Terafab precursors:** Jo Bhakdi notes that Tesla is currently partnering with Samsung on its AI5 and AI6 chips, which he describes as precursors to the Terafab initiative. Tesla is also working with TSMC. However, he argues that both Samsung and TSMC present strategic supply chain vulnerabilities — Samsung as a South Korean asset and TSMC as a Taiwanese company at risk of Chinese action — reinforcing the case for onshoring chip manufacturing through a company like Intel.

4. **Hyperscaler energy costs driving demand for space-based compute:** Jo Bhakdi argues that the $670 billion being spent by major hyperscalers (Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Google) on terrestrial data center buildout in 2026 is running into a hard ceiling: energy constraints. He states that AI data centers already consume 7% of total U.S. energy, and projects that as this figure grows, terrestrial energy costs will rise sharply. He presents space-based AI inference — powered by solar satellites — as the solution, claiming it will be approximately 40–60% cheaper than terrestrial compute once launch costs fall below $200 per kilogram to orbit, which he expects with Starship version 3 or version 4.

5. **Terafab's civilizational scope and chip manufacturing as the missing piece:** Jo Bhakdi describes Terafab as the largest chip manufacturing site on the planet, intended to supply chips for AI satellites, Optimus robots, and eventually lunar manufacturing operations. He emphasizes that SpaceX and Tesla/xAI currently have no chip manufacturing capability of their own, calling this the "missing piece" of the entire equation. He envisions a future where chips are manufactured on the moon using a lunar mass driver — a magnetic acceleration system — to deliver satellites into space at very low energy cost, potentially in the 2030s.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus as a key pillar of the space infrastructure vision:** Jo Bhakdi lists Optimus as one of the essential components of Elon Musk's long-term plan, alongside Starship and large-scale solar manufacturing. He frames Optimus's role specifically as maintaining the satellite infrastructure in space — handling the physical upkeep of what would be an enormous orbital network — rather than focusing on its near-term terrestrial applications.

Notable quotes and data:
- Intel's market cap cited at approximately $250 billion.
- Hyperscalers (Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Google) spending $670 billion on data center buildout in 2026.
- AI data centers currently consuming approximately 7% of total U.S. energy.
- SpaceX AI satellite mini described as a 100 kW design.
- Jo Bhakdi's threshold for space-based compute becoming economically superior: launch costs falling below $200 per kilogram to orbit.
- Jo Bhakdi's estimate: space-based data centers will be approximately 40–60% cheaper than terrestrial alternatives once that launch cost threshold is crossed.
- Starship version 3 (or at latest version 4) expected to reach commercial viability potentially by end of 2026, per Jo Bhakdi.
- Tesla currently partnering with Samsung on AI5 and AI6 chips as Terafab precursors.
- Lunar gravity described as approximately six times less than Earth's.
- Jo Bhakdi's timeline for lunar manufacturing operations: the 2030s.
- *"This is not anymore a business… This is the fundamental scaffolding of a civilization."*
- *"Intel is the perfect match to become a part of Tesla in my opinion."*
- *"I would not be surprised if Intel ends up as Tesla at some point in the future."*

articles.title: LIVE: Iran Crisis Update, Tesla Stock Weekly And AGI Breaking News: Pioneer Academy #5
articles.body:
This video is a live Pioneer Academy session hosted by Jo Bhakdi covering three main topics: a geopolitical analysis of the U.S.-Iran crisis and its market implications, a Tesla stock outlook and options strategy discussion, and a brief segment on AGI developments (particularly Anthropic's unreleased "Mythos" model). The core thesis is that despite near-term macro headwinds from the Iran situation, Tesla is approaching a sentiment-driven bottom, and the long-term bull case centered on Cybercab scaling, FSD expansion, and a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger remains intact.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD 14.3 Release Disappoints Market Expectations:** Jo Bhakdi notes that Tesla's FSD version 14.3 release contributed to negative sentiment because the market had expected more — specifically, hopes that the robotaxi and Cybercab launch would accompany it. Elon Musk subsequently posted that version 15 would be much better, which the market interpreted as goalpost-shifting. Jo suggests that version 15 is likely needed before meaningful unsupervised scaling occurs, though he cautions against betting on any specific version number.

2. **FSD Approved in the Netherlands — First EU Country:** A Friday afternoon bump in Tesla's stock was attributed to news that FSD received regulatory approval in the Netherlands, marking the first EU country to approve it. Jo characterizes this as expected and on-schedule, but notes it opens the door for further EU approvals and is an important milestone regardless.

3. **Unsupervised FSD Scaling Remains the Key Catalyst:** Jo emphasizes that the critical unknown is when unsupervised FSD will scale commercially. He expects the upcoming earnings call to be vague on this topic, with Tesla management likely saying they are making "tremendous progress" and that scaling is a function of continuous safety improvements rather than committing to a date. He believes until unsupervised scaling is confirmed, leaps-based options strategies carry meaningful time-decay risk.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab Production Is Active but Supervised Only:** Jo Bhakdi references drone footage and reporting by Joe Tegtmeyer showing 30 to 60 Cybercabs coming out of the factory every single day. He notes Cybercabs are being spotted in cities including Kansas, Chicago, Boston, New York, Texas, Arizona, California, and Florida. However, he acknowledges that unsupervised deployment has not yet scaled, which was the specific expectation he had for the April–May timeframe that he now admits was likely wrong.

2. **Robotaxi Tracker Shows Stagnant Unsupervised Count:** Jo pulls up the robotaxi tracker during the session and notes the unsupervised vehicle count is at approximately 10, with growth described as decelerating. He acknowledges this is not a dramatic or reliable data point but reflects the slow pace of unsupervised expansion.

3. **Cybercab Scaling as the Bridge to SpaceX/Optimus Revenue:** In the context of a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger, Jo argues that Cybercab revenue can serve as the financial bridge between Tesla's current valuation and the longer-term revenue streams from SpaceX and Optimus. He suggests Cybercab scaling could drive Tesla's market cap from roughly $1 trillion to $2–3 trillion relatively quickly, which would matter significantly for merger exchange ratios.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Tesla Stock Has Declined Significantly From Recent Highs:** Jo notes Tesla's stock has dropped from approximately $390 down to current levels, a significant slide over roughly three months, despite ongoing FSD progress and Cybercab production ramping. He draws a comparison to the same period last year when Tesla fell from around $420–430 all the way to $220–230, arguing the current decline is less severe.

## Market & Competition
1. **Jo Calls a Sentiment-Driven Bottom for Tesla:** Jo's primary market thesis for the session is that Tesla sentiment is now bad enough to mark a bottom. He states he is "getting very confident that Tesla will have a very hard time dropping more from here" and describes this as his big call — that it is probably time to "absolutely double down." He caveats this with macro risk from the Iran situation but argues that strategic escalation in Iran is very unlikely given the domestic political consequences for the Trump administration.

2. **Tesla-SpaceX Merger Thesis Remains High Conviction:** Jo argues the probability of a Tesla-SpaceX merger is approximately 99.9%, citing the convergence of the AI singularity, the need for unified energy and compute infrastructure, and the alignment of national security interests under the Trump administration. He contends that managing energy and chip bottlenecks for AGI separately across two companies is inefficient and that Elon Musk understands time — not money or ideas — is the binding constraint.

3. **SpaceX IPO Viewed as Overpriced Relative to Tesla:** Jo states he will not buy SpaceX at its IPO price, calling it "too expensive compared to Tesla" and expressing near-certainty that SpaceX shares will be available cheaper than the IPO price at some point after listing. He also notes that a SpaceX IPO could cause some Tesla holders to liquidate shares, creating a temporary drag on Tesla's price.

4. **AGI Inflection — Anthropic Mythos and the Singularity:** Jo discusses Anthropic's unreleased coding model called "Mythos," describing it as potentially reaching artificial super intelligence in coding. He explains Anthropic chose not to release it publicly and instead launched "Project Glasswing," giving access only to approximately 40 major software corporations (including Microsoft and Salesforce) to patch cybersecurity vulnerabilities before any wider release. He connects this to a broader thesis that the AI singularity has already begun in earnest, with 2027 as a rough inflection point, and that this creates unlimited demand for energy and inference chips — the two bottlenecks that make the Tesla-SpaceX merger strategically necessary.

Notable quotes and data:
- Jo Bhakdi on the Tesla bottom: "I'm getting very confident that Tesla will have a very hard time dropping more from here."
- Joe Tegtmeyer reportedly shows 30 to 60 Cybercabs coming out of the factory every single day via drone footage on X.
- Unsupervised robotaxi count on the robotaxi tracker shown live: approximately 10 vehicles.
- FSD paid adoption rate mentioned casually: "I think we are now at like double digits like 18% or something" — stated with uncertainty.
- Tesla stock decline referenced: from approximately $390 down to current levels (session recorded April 10, 2026).
- Last year comparison: Tesla fell from ~$420–430 to ~$220–230 in the same period of 2025; current decline considered less severe at ~$340.
- Anthropic's ARR reportedly went from $8 billion to $30 billion in roughly one month due to agent adoption.
- Nvidia stock referenced as approaching $190, described as "much safer than Tesla, but not as much upside."
- Jo's probability estimate on Tesla-SpaceX merger: "roughly 99.9%."
- Project Glasswing: Anthropic's restricted release program giving Mythos model access to ~40 major corporations for cybersecurity patching prior to public release.
- Netherlands FSD approval: first EU country to approve FSD, described as "expected and on time."

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-04-10)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts are headlined by two high-signal autonomous driving developments: Tesla's FSD daily mileage surging to 19.2 million miles per day (up from 14.4M just two months ago), and a tease that tomorrow could be a "massive day for FSD in Europe." The Robotaxi app also received a meaningful UI update, signaling continued operational refinement. EV-related posts were secondary, covering Model Y L international launches, a price increase in South Korea, and shifting delivery timelines in Australia.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD Mileage Milestone — Fleet Utilization Surging:** Tesla updated its FSD miles tracker to reflect a larger vehicle fleet and increased FSD adoption. The fleet is now averaging **19.2 million FSD miles per day**, up from **14.4 million miles per day** a couple of months ago — a roughly 33% increase in a short window. Merritt notes this equates to approximately 1,000 miles every 4.5 seconds. This is a meaningful signal for both the autonomous driving thesis (wider adoption, more training data accumulation) and as a proxy for FSD attach rate growth. Higher daily miles also feed directly into Tesla's safety-per-mile narrative and improve the real-world dataset advantage over competitors.

2. **FSD Europe — Potential Catalyst Tomorrow (April 11):** Merritt posted cryptically that April 11, 2026 is "potentially a massive day for FSD in Europe," without elaborating further. This is a high-interest teaser with no additional specifics provided. Given the regulatory complexity of FSD approval in European markets, any approval or supervised FSD launch in Europe would be a significant catalyst for Tesla's international autonomous driving expansion. Investors should watch for announcements on April 11.

3. **Robotaxi App Update — Operational Refinements:** Tesla updated its Robotaxi app with several notable changes: a new **tips section** showing available seat count, informing riders that vehicle lights will pulse upon arrival, and a disclosure that Tesla may use the **interior cabin camera for safety monitoring**. The app also received a darker visual appearance. These changes suggest Tesla is actively iterating on the rider experience and safety disclosure framework ahead of broader deployment — consistent with a service approaching more public-facing scale.

4. **Model Y L International Expansion — Mixed Demand Signals:** Tesla officially launched the larger **Model Y L in Israel**, with first deliveries beginning in June. However, in Australia, estimated delivery dates for new Model Y L orders have **pushed out to July–August 2026**, slipping from the prior May–June window — possibly indicating production constraints or logistics prioritization. Meanwhile, Tesla raised the price of the Model Y L in **South Korea by 7.7%**, which could reflect FX adjustments, demand strength, or tariff pass-throughs. Tesla also discontinued the white interior on all Model Y Premium trims built at **Giga Shanghai**, replacing it with the new "Zen Grey" interior across markets including Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, Japan, and the Philippines.

5. **Market & Competition — Legacy Automakers Alarmed by China:** A high-engagement post (6.3K likes, 1.2K reposts) highlighted stark statements from Toyota and Honda CEOs about Chinese EV competition. Toyota's CEO warned "unless things change, we will not survive," and Honda's CEO stated "we have no chance against this" after visiting China. While not directly about Tesla, this underscores the competitive pressure reshaping the global auto market — a dynamic that could benefit Tesla's positioning as a technology-first EV/AV company relative to legacy OEMs. Separately, Tesla reportedly added **China-based Sunwoda** to its global battery supply chain, introducing LFP battery technology focused on faster charging — a supply chain diversification move.

6. **Waymo/Waze Pothole Partnership — Competitor Activity:** Waymo announced a partnership with Waze to use autonomous fleet data to help cities detect and repair potholes, launching pilots in San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Austin, and Atlanta. This is a competitor development worth monitoring — Waymo is actively expanding its geographic footprint across five major U.S. cities while building municipal relationships. For Tesla's robotaxi thesis, Waymo's multi-city presence reinforces the competitive race for urban AV market share.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The sharp acceleration in FSD daily miles (19.2M vs. 14.4M two months ago) and the pending potential FSD Europe catalyst are strong forward signals for Tesla's autonomous driving thesis, while Robotaxi app updates suggest active operational scaling.

articles.title: Everyone Is Wrong About Tesla FSD v14.3
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel discusses the release of FSD v14.3, arguing that the broader online reaction dismissing it as another overpromise is wrong. Host Herbert is joined by Phil (a founding engineer at Rivian with Apple engineering management experience) and Cern Basher (a chartered financial analyst running Brilliant Advice wealth management) to break down what the update actually delivers and why it matters for unsupervised robotaxi deployment. The core thesis is that v14.3's two most significant changes — a 20% faster reaction time and a complete rewrite of the AI compiler and runtime from the ground up — together form the foundation needed for unsupervised robotaxi at scale, without needing to wait for version 15.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD v14.3 reaction time is now approximately 0.2 seconds:** Video analysis by "AI Driver" (a prominent FSD tester) found that v14.3 reacted to a changing traffic light in just 2/10 of a second from the moment the light turned yellow to when the car began controlling for it. For context, the industry standard reaction time used in accident reconstructions is 1.5 seconds for the full window from detecting a threat to physically applying brakes. Even an above-average human driver reacting in one second is still 5 to 7 times slower than v14.3. Elite sprinters, by comparison, are disqualified for false starts if they react in under one-tenth of a second, meaning FSD is now approaching the absolute physiological limit of human reaction capability.

2. **The AI compiler and runtime were rewritten from the ground up using MLIR:** Tesla's release notes confirm the rewrite was accomplished using MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation), which Phil explains allows Tesla engineers to take an abstract, system-wide view of where compute latency actually occurs — primarily in memory loads rather than in raw computation itself. By optimizing how data flows through the neural network stack (targeting approximately 36 inference cycles per second), the team eliminated bottlenecks that previously constrained both reaction time and model iteration speed. Phil speculates this groundwork was likely added to the roadmap in early fall and was a key reason the release took longer than expected.

3. **The runtime rewrite enables faster future model iteration:** Both the release notes and AI Driver's analysis highlight that a critical but underreported line item is the improvement to model iteration speed. Phil explains that with the previous custom-built runtime that had been incrementally patched over years, there was no good system-wide optimizer. The new architecture now allows Tesla to rapidly iterate on the underlying AI model — adding reinforcement learning cases, increasing vision resolution, and eventually scaling parameter count — without the bottlenecks of the old system constraining each update cycle.

4. **v14.3 introduces some regressions alongside its improvements:** AI Driver noted that some of the indecisive, jerky steering behaviors from early v14 builds have returned in v14.3, particularly at straightforward unprotected left turns and flashing crosswalks without pedestrians. He attributes this directly to the speed of v14.3's decision-to-control-output pipeline: the system is now so fast it appears to be simultaneously weighing many more options before committing, which creates perceptible hesitation. The panelists agree this is expected from a ground-up rewrite and will be addressed in point releases (e.g., 14.3.1, 14.3.2) before a full wide release.

5. **Reinforcement learning drove a large portion of the v14.3 improvements:** Cern Basher and Phil both emphasize that many of the specific scenario improvements listed in the release notes — improved handling of small animals, school buses, emergency vehicles, rare objects, complex intersections, yellow light stopping, and pothole avoidance (upcoming) — are all products of reinforcement learning (RL) cases built from incidents observed by Tesla's safety drivers in the robotaxi program. Phil describes a "human pipeline" that has matured significantly since the robotaxi program began, where safety observers identify edge cases, engineers construct RL scenarios, run them through the simulator, and integrate the results into the model.

6. **Version 15 will be the large-model, 10x parameter release — but is not required for unsupervised robotaxi:** Elon Musk confirmed in a post that v15 will be the "large model" with the 10x parameter increase, and that the small model has been iterating so fast the large model has not yet caught up. However, all three panelists agree that Elon did not say v15 is a prerequisite for unsupervised robotaxi deployment. Phil notes that increasing parameters 10x would be meaningless without first having an optimized runtime to support it on Hardware 4, which is exactly what v14.3 delivers. Herbert states he has predicted that fully unsupervised operation in Austin could happen as early as April 2026.

7. **Hardware 3 vehicles may receive a "v14 light" but are unlikely to run unsupervised:** Cern raised the possibility that the more efficient new runtime could enable a lighter version of upgraded FSD to run on Hardware 3 vehicles, citing Tesla's prior earnings call comments about seeing "a potential pathway" for Hardware 3. Phil acknowledges this speculation is reasonable given that engineering under hardware constraints often produces optimizations that benefit all platforms. However, Phil is firm in his prediction that Hardware 3 vehicles will never run unsupervised — neither in the robotaxi network nor in a customer scenario — because the compute environment is simply too limited for that level of operation.

8. **The improved driver monitoring system upgrade is targeted at supervised Hardware 3 use:** The upcoming feature to improve driver monitoring system sensitivity — with better eye gaze tracking, eyewear handling, and variable lighting accuracy — is interpreted by Phil as primarily a Hardware 3 feature. Since unsupervised FSD is not expected to come to Hardware 3, Tesla wants the supervised experience on those vehicles to be as accurate and non-intrusive as possible, only intervening when genuinely necessary. Cern also notes practical annoyances like sunglasses or looking at the in-car screen triggering false attention warnings, which this update aims to address.

## Robotaxi

1. **v14.3's faster reaction time directly addresses robotaxi safety incidents:** Cern specifically calls out that the one incident Tesla's robotaxi had to report between January 15 and February 15, 2026 — a front vehicle stopping suddenly, resulting in a bumper touch — is exactly the type of scenario that v14.3's 20% faster reaction time would prevent. He also notes that Waymo's well-known highway collision issues stem not from lidar failing to detect cutting-in vehicles, but from slow reaction time after detection. The 0.2-second reaction window would effectively eliminate that class of accident.

2. **Destination handling with reasoning was added first because robotaxi requires it:** Herbert highlights that v14.3 added reasoning specifically to destination handling (pickup and drop-off), with broader reasoning expansion to other driving behaviors listed as an upcoming improvement. Phil explains that this feature was essentially absent from consumer FSD data because regular FSD users never needed the car to autonomously pick them up or drop them off — they simply took control at the end of a trip. The robotaxi operation mode requires precise, safe, and efficient pickup and drop-off logic, and this is one of the areas most specific to the robotaxi use case that had to be built from near-scratch using robotaxi operational data.

3. **Scaling robotaxi requires minimizing remote operations calls:** Phil makes the point that whatever edge cases remain in FSD — trees blocking roads, unusual drop-off situations, system degradation — must be handled autonomously by the vehicle rather than escalating to a remote operations center. He argues Tesla is actively thinking about what their operations center would look like at 1,000x, 2,000x, or 5,000x fleet scale, and that the goal is to reduce calls to only truly critical situations. The v14.3 feature improving handling of temporary system degradations and automatic recovery without driver intervention is directly relevant to this requirement.

4. **Tesla is prioritizing robotaxi unsupervised deployment ahead of consumer unsupervised FSD:** The panel agrees that Tesla's internal priority order is robotaxi-first, consumer unsupervised second. Phil argues there is a distinct and complex set of consumer-side items required for customer-unsupervised FSD that are simply lower priority right now. Cern and Phil also note a business logic rationale: scaling robotaxi first generates revenue and cash flow needed to absorb the inevitable litigation from edge-case accidents — a point Elon himself made publicly, noting that Tesla will likely avoid 90% of accidents but will still get sued for the unavoidable 10%.

5. **Safety observer pipeline has matured significantly since summer 2025 robotaxi launch:** Phil describes the early days of the robotaxi program as "a bit of chaos" in terms of how incidents were reported, categorized, and fed back into the engineering process. He believes the human pipeline — from safety driver observation through to RL case construction and model integration — has now matured to a level of efficiency that is enabling the quality and breadth of scenario coverage seen in v14.3. This maturation is described as one of the less-discussed but important reasons why the robotaxi program is now positioned to scale.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD v14.3 reaction time measured at approximately **0.2 seconds** from yellow light detection to control output, vs. industry standard **1.5 seconds** for human accident reconstruction and **1 second** for an above-average alert driver — making FSD **5 to 7 times faster** than an above-average human.
- Elite sprinters are disqualified for false starts if they react in under **0.1 seconds**, meaning FSD at 0.2 seconds is approaching human physiological limits.
- Tesla's AI runtime now targets approximately **36 inference cycles per second**, potentially expandable to 60.
- Elon Musk: *"Our rate of investment with the small model has been so fast that the large model has not yet caught up. V15 will be the large model."*
- AI Driver: *"We finally crossed the point where it's basically factual that driving with FSD is significantly safer than driving yourself... I actually feel exposed when driving manually."*
- Phil: *"If you increase the parameter count by 10x and then were left with less than optimal input data or less than optimal runtime, then what was the point in the first place?"*
- Cern: *"I wonder out loud right now — does a 20% faster reaction time reduce accidents by 50%, 60%, 80%?"*
- Herbert predicts Tesla could announce **100% unsupervised operation in Austin as early as April 2026**.
- Tesla robotaxi reported **one incident between January 15 and February 15** (a bumper touch from a sudden stop ahead).
- The v14.3 rewrite used **MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation)** for the AI compiler and runtime.

articles.title: Tesla Is the New iPhone - Most People Don't See It
articles.body:
This video from the channel "brighterwithherbert" argues that buying a Tesla in 2026 is analogous to buying an iPhone in 2010 — a pivotal moment where the dominant technology is proven, but mass adoption has barely begun. The host draws an extended parallel between the smartphone revolution and the coming autonomous vehicle transition, framing Tesla as the iPhone and traditional human-driven cars as the BlackBerry. The core thesis is that smart cars will inevitably replace dumb cars, and investors or consumers who recognize this now are positioned similarly to early Apple investors.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD trajectory mirrors iPhone improvement curve:** The host traces FSD's evolution from 6 million miles of driving data in 2021 to 9 billion miles at the time of the video. He notes that FSD has progressed from crashing every few miles to completing 44% of all drives door-to-door with zero takeovers. He argues this rapid improvement trajectory is the defining characteristic — not where the technology is on day one, but the speed and direction of progress, which he calls "the iPhone trajectory."
