2. **The AI compiler and runtime were rewritten from the ground up using MLIR:** Tesla's release notes confirm the rewrite was accomplished using MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation), which Phil explains allows Tesla engineers to take an abstract, system-wide view of where compute latency actually occurs — primarily in memory loads rather than in raw computation itself. By optimizing how data flows through the neural network stack (targeting approximately 36 inference cycles per second), the team eliminated bottlenecks that previously constrained both reaction time and model iteration speed. Phil speculates this groundwork was likely added to the roadmap in early fall and was a key reason the release took longer than expected.

3. **The runtime rewrite enables faster future model iteration:** Both the release notes and AI Driver's analysis highlight that a critical but underreported line item is the improvement to model iteration speed. Phil explains that with the previous custom-built runtime that had been incrementally patched over years, there was no good system-wide optimizer. The new architecture now allows Tesla to rapidly iterate on the underlying AI model — adding reinforcement learning cases, increasing vision resolution, and eventually scaling parameter count — without the bottlenecks of the old system constraining each update cycle.

4. **v14.3 introduces some regressions alongside its improvements:** AI Driver noted that some of the indecisive, jerky steering behaviors from early v14 builds have returned in v14.3, particularly at straightforward unprotected left turns and flashing crosswalks without pedestrians. He attributes this directly to the speed of v14.3's decision-to-control-output pipeline: the system is now so fast it appears to be simultaneously weighing many more options before committing, which creates perceptible hesitation. The panelists agree this is expected from a ground-up rewrite and will be addressed in point releases (e.g., 14.3.1, 14.3.2) before a full wide release.

5. **Reinforcement learning drove a large portion of the v14.3 improvements:** Cern Basher and Phil both emphasize that many of the specific scenario improvements listed in the release notes — improved handling of small animals, school buses, emergency vehicles, rare objects, complex intersections, yellow light stopping, and pothole avoidance (upcoming) — are all products of reinforcement learning (RL) cases built from incidents observed by Tesla's safety drivers in the robotaxi program. Phil describes a "human pipeline" that has matured significantly since the robotaxi program began, where safety observers identify edge cases, engineers construct RL scenarios, run them through the simulator, and integrate the results into the model.

6. **Version 15 will be the large-model, 10x parameter release — but is not required for unsupervised robotaxi:** Elon Musk confirmed in a post that v15 will be the "large model" with the 10x parameter increase, and that the small model has been iterating so fast the large model has not yet caught up. However, all three panelists agree that Elon did not say v15 is a prerequisite for unsupervised robotaxi deployment. Phil notes that increasing parameters 10x would be meaningless without first having an optimized runtime to support it on Hardware 4, which is exactly what v14.3 delivers. Herbert states he has predicted that fully unsupervised operation in Austin could happen as early as April 2026.

7. **Hardware 3 vehicles may receive a "v14 light" but are unlikely to run unsupervised:** Cern raised the possibility that the more efficient new runtime could enable a lighter version of upgraded FSD to run on Hardware 3 vehicles, citing Tesla's prior earnings call comments about seeing "a potential pathway" for Hardware 3. Phil acknowledges this speculation is reasonable given that engineering under hardware constraints often produces optimizations that benefit all platforms. However, Phil is firm in his prediction that Hardware 3 vehicles will never run unsupervised — neither in the robotaxi network nor in a customer scenario — because the compute environment is simply too limited for that level of operation.

8. **The improved driver monitoring system upgrade is targeted at supervised Hardware 3 use:** The upcoming feature to improve driver monitoring system sensitivity — with better eye gaze tracking, eyewear handling, and variable lighting accuracy — is interpreted by Phil as primarily a Hardware 3 feature. Since unsupervised FSD is not expected to come to Hardware 3, Tesla wants the supervised experience on those vehicles to be as accurate and non-intrusive as possible, only intervening when genuinely necessary. Cern also notes practical annoyances like sunglasses or looking at the in-car screen triggering false attention warnings, which this update aims to address.

## Robotaxi

1. **v14.3's faster reaction time directly addresses robotaxi safety incidents:** Cern specifically calls out that the one incident Tesla's robotaxi had to report between January 15 and February 15, 2026 — a front vehicle stopping suddenly, resulting in a bumper touch — is exactly the type of scenario that v14.3's 20% faster reaction time would prevent. He also notes that Waymo's well-known highway collision issues stem not from lidar failing to detect cutting-in vehicles, but from slow reaction time after detection. The 0.2-second reaction window would effectively eliminate that class of accident.

2. **Destination handling with reasoning was added first because robotaxi requires it:** Herbert highlights that v14.3 added reasoning specifically to destination handling (pickup and drop-off), with broader reasoning expansion to other driving behaviors listed as an upcoming improvement. Phil explains that this feature was essentially absent from consumer FSD data because regular FSD users never needed the car to autonomously pick them up or drop them off — they simply took control at the end of a trip. The robotaxi operation mode requires precise, safe, and efficient pickup and drop-off logic, and this is one of the areas most specific to the robotaxi use case that had to be built from near-scratch using robotaxi operational data.

3. **Scaling robotaxi requires minimizing remote operations calls:** Phil makes the point that whatever edge cases remain in FSD — trees blocking roads, unusual drop-off situations, system degradation — must be handled autonomously by the vehicle rather than escalating to a remote operations center. He argues Tesla is actively thinking about what their operations center would look like at 1,000x, 2,000x, or 5,000x fleet scale, and that the goal is to reduce calls to only truly critical situations. The v14.3 feature improving handling of temporary system degradations and automatic recovery without driver intervention is directly relevant to this requirement.

4. **Tesla is prioritizing robotaxi unsupervised deployment ahead of consumer unsupervised FSD:** The panel agrees that Tesla's internal priority order is robotaxi-first, consumer unsupervised second. Phil argues there is a distinct and complex set of consumer-side items required for customer-unsupervised FSD that are simply lower priority right now. Cern and Phil also note a business logic rationale: scaling robotaxi first generates revenue and cash flow needed to absorb the inevitable litigation from edge-case accidents — a point Elon himself made publicly, noting that Tesla will likely avoid 90% of accidents but will still get sued for the unavoidable 10%.

5. **Safety observer pipeline has matured significantly since summer 2025 robotaxi launch:** Phil describes the early days of the robotaxi program as "a bit of chaos" in terms of how incidents were reported, categorized, and fed back into the engineering process. He believes the human pipeline — from safety driver observation through to RL case construction and model integration — has now matured to a level of efficiency that is enabling the quality and breadth of scenario coverage seen in v14.3. This maturation is described as one of the less-discussed but important reasons why the robotaxi program is now positioned to scale.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD v14.3 reaction time measured at approximately **0.2 seconds** from yellow light detection to control output, vs. industry standard **1.5 seconds** for human accident reconstruction and **1 second** for an above-average alert driver — making FSD **5 to 7 times faster** than an above-average human.
- Elite sprinters are disqualified for false starts if they react in under **0.1 seconds**, meaning FSD at 0.2 seconds is approaching human physiological limits.
- Tesla's AI runtime now targets approximately **36 inference cycles per second**, potentially expandable to 60.
- Elon Musk: *"Our rate of investment with the small model has been so fast that the large model has not yet caught up. V15 will be the large model."*
- AI Driver: *"We finally crossed the point where it's basically factual that driving with FSD is significantly safer than driving yourself... I actually feel exposed when driving manually."*
- Phil: *"If you increase the parameter count by 10x and then were left with less than optimal input data or less than optimal runtime, then what was the point in the first place?"*
- Cern: *"I wonder out loud right now — does a 20% faster reaction time reduce accidents by 50%, 60%, 80%?"*
- Herbert predicts Tesla could announce **100% unsupervised operation in Austin as early as April 2026**.
- Tesla robotaxi reported **one incident between January 15 and February 15** (a bumper touch from a sudden stop ahead).
- The v14.3 rewrite used **MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation)** for the AI compiler and runtime.

2026-04-11.title: Tesla Is the New iPhone - Most People Don't See It
2026-04-11.body:
This video from the channel "brighterwithherbert" argues that buying a Tesla in 2026 is analogous to buying an iPhone in 2010 — a pivotal moment where the dominant technology is proven, but mass adoption has barely begun. The host draws an extended parallel between the smartphone revolution and the coming autonomous vehicle transition, framing Tesla as the iPhone and traditional human-driven cars as the BlackBerry. The core thesis is that smart cars will inevitably replace dumb cars, and investors or consumers who recognize this now are positioned similarly to early Apple investors.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD trajectory mirrors iPhone improvement curve:** The host traces FSD's evolution from 6 million miles of driving data in 2021 to 9 billion miles at the time of the video. He notes that FSD has progressed from crashing every few miles to completing 44% of all drives door-to-door with zero takeovers. He argues this rapid improvement trajectory is the defining characteristic — not where the technology is on day one, but the speed and direction of progress, which he calls "the iPhone trajectory."

2. **FSD safety data and independent verification gap:** The host cites Tesla's own data showing FSD is roughly nine times safer than the average human driver. He also references Waymo's peer-reviewed data showing 90% fewer serious injury crashes than human drivers over 170 million miles. He explicitly acknowledges a credibility gap, noting that Tesla's FSD safety data is self-reported while Waymo's has been peer-reviewed, and that until Tesla opens up to the same level of independent verification, questions around its safety numbers will persist.

3. **FSD global expansion in progress:** The host states that FSD is currently live in seven countries, with Europe described as pending and Japan and Israel in testing phases. He frames these as the early data points on an adoption curve that has "basically not started" globally.

4. **Insurance companies already pricing in FSD safety:** As a concrete market signal, the host notes that Lemonade Insurance is offering 50% off per-mile rates when FSD is engaged, citing this as evidence that the financial industry is already recognizing the safety differential of autonomous driving.

## Robotaxi

5. **Austin robotaxi service already live, expansion to 18 cities planned:** The host states that Tesla is running a robotaxi service in Austin with no safety driver, and that expansion to 18 cities is coming soon. He positions the Austin deployment as the equivalent of the iPhone's App Store launch — proof the platform works, before mass adoption begins.

6. **Tesla's robotaxi target fare under 20 cents per mile:** The host references Tesla's stated target of under 20 cents per mile for robotaxi rides, arguing this would make the cost so low that car ownership stops making financial sense for many people. He contrasts this with the average American spending approximately $12,000 per year on car ownership (payments, insurance, gas, maintenance).

7. **Cybercab production is starting:** The host mentions that Cybercab production is starting in 2026, citing it alongside the Austin robotaxi launch and global FSD expansion as evidence that Tesla is at a commercialization inflection point.

8. **New York blocked robotaxi expansion:** As a regulatory headwind, the host notes that in February 2026, Governor Hochul scrapped a robotaxi proposal for New York State following pushback from the Taxi Workers Alliance (representing 28,000 drivers) and the Teamsters. He identifies union opposition — specifically Maravi Desai of the New York Taxi Workers Alliance and John Samuelson of the Transport Workers Union International — as the present-day equivalent of BlackBerry executives dismissing the iPhone. He argues this creates a roadmap: permissive states will adopt first, resistant ones later.

## Electric Vehicles

9. **Cars as assets, not expenses — V2G and distributed compute:** The host argues that a Tesla capable of running AI compute while parked and selling energy back to the grid (V2G) transforms a car from an expense into a revenue-generating asset. He describes this as a fundamental shift in the economics of car ownership, with features like FSD, V2G, and distributed compute described as either already existing or coming this year or next year (2026–2027).

## Market & Competition

10. **Tesla's competitive moat vs. a crowded autonomous field:** The host acknowledges that unlike Apple in 2007, Tesla faces serious competition — naming Waymo, Zoox, and "a dozen Chinese companies" all working on autonomy. He concedes the iPhone-versus-BlackBerry framing may overstate Tesla's lead. However, he argues that no competitor matches Tesla's combination of fleet scale, driving data, manufacturing capacity, and vertical integration, giving Tesla what he characterizes as the biggest head start.

11. **Slower transition than smartphones — structural differences acknowledged:** The host directly addresses the imperfection of the iPhone analogy. He notes the car replacement cycle (a decade or more) is far longer than phones (two to three years), meaning full autonomous adoption could take 10 to 20 years rather than 5. He also flags that robo taxis require government regulatory approval in a way iPhones never did, creating city-by-city and state-by-state friction that smartphones never faced.

12. **Tesla's current valuation reflects the thesis divide:** The host observes that Tesla is currently trading at approximately 330 times earnings, noting that this price "looks expensive if you only see the car business" but looks completely different when the robotaxi, energy, AI, and robotics businesses are included. He frames this as the fundamental investor question: are you pricing a car company, or are you pricing the autonomous transition?

Notable quotes and data:
- "FSD went from 6 million miles in 2021 to 9 billion miles today."
- "44% of all drives completed door-to-door with zero takeovers."
- "Waymo has published peer-reviewed data showing their cars have 90% fewer serious injury crashes than human drivers over 170 million miles."
- "Tesla's data shows FSD is roughly nine times safer than the average human."
- "Lemonade's offering 50% off per-mile rates when FSD is driving."
- Tesla's robotaxi target: "under 20 cents a mile."
- "The average American spends about $12,000 a year on their car."
- "Over 40,000 people die in car crashes every year in the United States alone, 90% caused by human error."
- "Studies project that the economic benefit of autonomous vehicles at over $900 billion per year from reduced accidents alone."
- "Roughly 30% of urban land in most American cities is parking."
- "In February 2026, Governor Hochul scrapped the entire robotaxi proposal for the state."
- "FSD is live in seven countries. Robotaxis running in Austin with no safety driver. Cybercab production is starting."
- "Global adoption of autonomous driving is basically at 0%. We're at the 2010 moment."
- Tesla currently trading at "330 times PE."
- Apple stock was "around $30 a share, split adjusted" in 2010; investors made "60 times their money over the next 15 years."
- Robotaxi expansion "expanding soon to 18 cities."

2026-04-11.title: High Gas Prices Are Becoming Tesla’s Best Salesman
2026-04-11.body:
This video is a casual conversational interview between Brian (Futurazza) and Will (Tesla Jigsaw), a UK-based EV advocate, discussing how rising fuel prices in the UK are making electric vehicles increasingly attractive to mainstream consumers. The conversation covers the cost comparison between petrol and electric driving, available EV incentives in the UK, the state of the used EV market, and the regulatory landscape pushing the UK toward full electrification by 2030.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **UK Petrol Prices Creating Strong EV Value Proposition:** Fuel costs in the UK have reached approximately £85 to fill up the average petrol family car, with diesel exceeding £100 per fill. Will notes that driving on home overnight electricity tariffs is roughly a tenth of the cost of petrol, making the financial case for switching to an EV extremely compelling for anyone with a driveway. Brian adds context for US viewers that the UK petrol price works out to approximately $7.63 per gallon based on a price of £1.52 per liter at Asda, with the pound trading at roughly $1.32–$1.35.

2. **Used EV Market in the UK Is Expanding and Affordable:** Will highlights that a used Model 3 can be purchased for under £10,000 on the secondhand market, and basic EV runarounds (BMW i3, Nissan Leaf, Renault Zoe) are available for as little as £2,000. He notes that his own used 2019 California-built Model 3 would have served his needs indefinitely, and that he and his household recently upgraded to a Model 3 Juniper (premium rear-wheel drive). Brian echoes that affordable used EVs in the $20,000–$25,000 range challenge the persistent myth that EVs are only for wealthy buyers.

3. **Real-World Savings Case Study:** Will shares the example of a friend driving a Volvo S60 2L petrol who spends just under £400 per month on fuel. Will calculated that switching to a Model 3 with home charging would save approximately £360 per month — enough to cover a PCP (personal contract purchase) finance payment on a Tesla with money left over. Even a Model 3 owner relying solely on the Supercharger network was still saving several hundred pounds per year compared to running a petrol car.

4. **UK EV Incentives — Electric Car Grant (ECG):** The UK's Electric Car Grant, launched in 2025, provides an automatic dealer discount on new battery electric vehicles priced under £37,000. Band one (greenest manufacturing/sustainability standards) offers £3,750 off, with approximately nine qualifying models. Band two (meets minimum sustainability criteria) offers £1,500 off, with over 40 qualifying models. Tesla vehicles do not currently qualify because the base Model 3 starts at £37,950 — just above the threshold — though Tesla's manufacturing sustainability would otherwise meet the criteria.

5. **Tesla's Own Incentive Response:** In lieu of qualifying for the ECG, Tesla is offering a £3,750 trade-in bonus (on top of the vehicle's trade-in value) on all new inventory Model 3 and Model Y vehicles, excluding performance variants. This offer runs from April to June 2026 with short delivery deadlines. It stacks with 0% finance available on non-performance base versions, and an additional £500 discount is available via referral links.

6. **Home Charging Incentives Are Limited for Homeowners:** Will explains that UK homeowners receive no government grant for home charger installation. However, renters, flat residents, and landlords can claim up to £500 per socket, and a workplace charger scheme offers up to £500 per socket for a maximum of 40 sockets per business, extended through March 2027. Octopus Energy is highlighted as a major player offering EV leasing, heat pumps, and public charging solutions including the Electroverse card, which provides 8% off charging across most of the UK's rapid charging network. A scheme called "Turbocharge" (via Octopus) installs charging points on pavements outside homes or on nearby lamp posts.

7. **VAT on Public Charging Nearing Reduction:** Brian and Will discuss the long-running campaign by the late Quentin Wilson and Faircharge to reduce the VAT rate on public EV charging from 20% down to 5% — matching the reduced rate applied to home electricity. A recent UK court ruling appears to have pointed toward adopting the domestic 5% VAT rate for public charging, suggesting this long-sought change may be imminent or already in motion.

## Market & Competition

1. **UK ZEV Mandate Sets 2030 Deadline for New Petrol/Diesel Sales:** The UK's Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate requires no new petrol or diesel car sales from 2030, a date that was previously shifted to 2035 before being moved back to 2030, creating significant supply chain uncertainty for automakers. A rising ZEV sales target requires 33% of manufacturer vehicle sales to be battery electric vehicles by 2026, with financial penalties for non-compliance. A pay-per-mile road charge for EVs is also being discussed for introduction by 2028, and EVs will begin paying Vehicle Excise Duty (road tax) going forward.

2. **Shifting Public Sentiment Toward EVs:** Will observes that EV adoption is visibly growing in his local area of Market Harborough, England, with at least 10 EVs on his street alone. He notes that geopolitical tensions involving Iran and resulting fuel price volatility are accelerating consumer interest in switching to electric. Brian notes that persistent misconceptions (range anxiety, explosion risk, battery replacement costs) remain a barrier but are slowly eroding as EVs become more common and financially appealing. The UK lacks a major domestic auto manufacturing base to protect, which has generally resulted in lower EV import barriers compared to other markets.

Notable quotes and data:
- Average UK petrol fill-up: approximately £85 for a petrol family car, over £100 for diesel
- UK petrol price at Asda: £1.52 per liter ≈ $7.63 per gallon (at ~$1.32–$1.35/£)
- Home charging cost vs. petrol: approximately one-tenth the cost on an overnight electricity tariff
- Used Model 3 available for under £10,000 in UK; basic EV runarounds available from £2,000
- Volvo S60 petrol owner spending ~£400/month on fuel; Model 3 switch would save ~£360/month
- Tesla UK trade-in bonus: £3,750 on top of trade-in value, April–June 2026, on Model 3 and Model Y (non-performance), stacks with 0% finance and £500 referral discount
- ECG Band 1: £3,750 off, ~9 qualifying models; Band 2: £1,500 off, 40+ qualifying models; price cap: £37,000
- Tesla Model 3 base price in UK: £37,950 (just above ECG threshold)
- Workplace charging grant: up to £500/socket, max 40 sockets per business, extended to March 2027
- Octopus Electroverse card: 8% discount on charging across most of UK rapid charging network
- UK ZEV mandate: 33% BEV sales required from manufacturers by 2026; no new petrol/diesel sales from 2030
- Pay-per-mile EV road charge proposed for introduction by 2028

2026-04-11.title: Why The REAL Plan For Tesla's Super Chip Factor (Terafab) Is CRAZY
2026-04-11.body:
This video from Jo Bhakdi's channel presents a sweeping strategic vision centered on the Terafab initiative — Tesla/SpaceX/xAI's plan to manufacture AI inference chips at massive scale and ultimately deploy space-based compute infrastructure. The core thesis is that this mission, while seemingly fantastical, is actually the *easiest* large-scale undertaking Elon Musk has ever attempted, precisely because Starship, FSD/robotaxi, and Optimus have already solved the harder foundational problems. Jo Bhakdi walks through the Terafab.ai website to illustrate the broader civilizational ambition, arguing that the convergence of AGI readiness, Starship's imminent viability, and Wall Street's institutional buy-in creates a rare "Goldilocks moment" of unlimited economic scaling potential.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD and Robotaxi as the Hard Problems Already Solved:** Jo Bhakdi argues that Full Self-Driving and the robotaxi stack represent some of the most difficult engineering challenges ever undertaken — solving problems that had never been solved before. He frames these as the *harder* precedents that make Terafab's chip manufacturing mission look trivial by comparison. The existence of a working FSD/robotaxi system is cited as one of the foundational prerequisites that makes the broader Terafab and space compute plan executable.

## Robotaxi
1. **Robotaxi as a Pillar of the Terafab Vision:** The Terafab.ai website, as described by Jo Bhakdi, explicitly lists robotaxis (and "robotrucking") as one of Tesla's core verticals that will generate massive inference compute demand. The dedicated inference chip designs being planned under Terafab are described as optimized for specific vertical stacks — with robotaxi explicitly named as one such vertical — rather than being general-purpose chips like Nvidia's Blackwell.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **1 Billion Optimus Units as a Civilizational Requirement:** The Terafab.ai website presents a figure of 1 billion Tesla Optimus robots as part of the infrastructure needed to achieve the broader galactic civilization ambition. Jo Bhakdi notes this number may be somewhat arbitrary — it could be 100 million or more — but emphasizes that demand for humanoid robots will be effectively unlimited. He highlights that Optimus robots are uniquely suited for space environments: they don't need sleep, don't need oxygen, and can function in extremely cold conditions such as on the Moon.

2. **Optimus as a Harder Problem Than Terafab:** Jo Bhakdi uses Optimus development as a benchmark for engineering difficulty. He argues that Optimus involved solving previously unsolved problems and building complicated supply chains for unknown components — making it far harder than designing and manufacturing inference chips. The fact that Optimus is already underway makes Terafab's chip mission comparatively straightforward.

## Market & Competition
1. **Terafab's Inference Chip Strategy vs. Nvidia:** Jo Bhakdi draws a sharp distinction between Nvidia's general-purpose training-and-inference chips (like Blackwell) and the simpler, mass-producible inference chips Tesla plans to manufacture under Terafab. He argues that for robotaxi, Optimus, and space compute, a complex all-in-one chip is unnecessary. Simpler inference chips optimized for specific vertical stacks can be mass-produced at scale with fewer R&D leaps. He describes the process as calling Intel or Samsung, hiring chip engineers, designing inference chips using open tools, and manufacturing them — characterizing it as "trivial" in terms of innovation risk.

2. **SpaceX's Dominance in Launch Capacity:** Jo Bhakdi states that SpaceX currently launches 90% of global mass to orbit even before Starship is operational. He projects that once Starship is active, that market share will rise to approximately 99% by 2030 at the latest. Starship is described as capable of transporting 150 tons to orbit and is expected to reduce the cost of mass to orbit by roughly 100x — from approximately $2,500 per kilogram with Falcon down to approximately $25 per kilogram at full scale. He suggests a near-term milestone of ~$200 per kilogram (a 10x reduction) could be achieved as early as next year (2027), which he says is sufficient to initiate the space-based compute business.

3. **Space Energy Economics as a Competitive Moat:** Jo Bhakdi explains that solar energy in space delivers approximately 40% more solar radiation than on Earth due to no atmospheric losses, and approximately five times more effective daily energy per panel due to constant 24/7 sun exposure if satellites are properly oriented. He argues this makes space-based compute fundamentally different from terrestrial AI compute: energy is effectively free, eliminating the energy efficiency constraints that Nvidia chips must meet for cost-sensitive earthbound customers. This creates an entirely independent engineering equation for Terafab's space chips.

4. **xAI's Hardware Edge:** The Terafab.ai website highlights xAI as having built the first gigawatt-scale AI training cluster. Jo Bhakdi notes this represents a meaningful hardware engineering advantage that competitors like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Microsoft do not possess.

5. **Wall Street Institutional Buy-In as the Third Goldilocks Dimension:** Jo Bhakdi expresses surprise and excitement that major institutional investors — including Fidelity's head of private equities and BlackRock — have apparently come to understand and endorse the Terafab/SpaceX vision. He cites the anticipated SpaceX IPO at a ~$2 trillion valuation as evidence of this institutional alignment. He frames this as the third leg of a "Goldilocks moment": AGI compute demand is here, Starship is nearly ready, and capital markets are on board.

6. **Tesla-Intel Collaboration:** Jo Bhakdi briefly references a separate video he made about Tesla and Intel entering a close manufacturing partnership related to chip production, suggesting this is a key near-term enabler for the Terafab chip manufacturing strategy.

Notable quotes and data:
- "There is no huge R&D leap required. There's no deep science required... It is trivial."
- "When you draw a diagram and say how big is something and how hard is it? There's nothing that Elon ever did that was bigger and easier than Terafab and space AI."
- SpaceX currently holds ~90% of global mass-to-orbit launch share; projected to reach ~99% by 2030
- Starship payload capacity: 150 tons to orbit
- Cost to orbit today (Falcon): ~$2,500/kg; projected long-term with Starship: ~$25/kg; near-term milestone: ~$200/kg
- Space solar flux: ~40% more radiation than Earth's surface; ~5x more effective daily energy per panel due to constant exposure
- xAI built the first gigawatt-scale AI training cluster
- Terafab.ai lists 1 billion Optimus robots as part of the civilizational build-out
- First AI compute satellite's compute cluster: reportedly ~100 kW (Jo Bhakdi notes he heard this from Elon but is uncertain)
- SpaceX IPO anticipated at ~$2 trillion valuation
- Elon Musk has worked on Starship for approximately 24 years (since 2002)
- Kardashev Type 1 civilization = harness all energy of one planet; Type 2 = all energy of a star; Type 3 = all energy of a galaxy

2026-04-11.title: Daily X Summary (2026-04-11)
2026-04-11.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts were dominated by a landmark regulatory breakthrough: FSD (Supervised) received its first-ever European approval in the Netherlands, with FSD V14 subscriptions launching at €99/month and Dutch regulators (RDW) issuing a notably positive safety endorsement. Alongside this, Tesla's FSD fleet activity hit a new high of 19.2 million miles per day, the Robotaxi app received a meaningful update hinting at near-term operational refinements, and the Model Y continued to demonstrate strong commercial momentum in China and new markets. The overall signal is strongly bullish for Tesla's autonomous driving thesis.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD (Supervised) Receives First European Approval — Netherlands Launches at €99/Month:** In the day's most significant development, Tesla announced that FSD (Supervised) has been officially approved by the Dutch regulatory authority (RDW) and will begin rolling out to customer vehicles in the Netherlands shortly. FSD subscriptions launched at €99/month, making this the first European country to receive regulatory clearance. Merritt emphasized this clears the path for approvals in other European countries and potentially an EU-wide rollout. The RDW issued a notably strong official statement, describing the system as "safer than other driver assistance systems" due to "continuous strict monitoring of the driver," and stating that "proper use of this driver's system makes a positive contribution to road safety." This regulatory endorsement from an EU-member authority carries significant weight as a template for broader European expansion. Dutch Tesla owners will go from Autopilot directly to FSD V14, which Merritt called a generational leap in capability overnight. This post reached 3.9K likes and 477 retweets, indicating high viral reach on a material claim.

2. **FSD Fleet Activity Surges to 19.2 Million Miles Per Day:** Tesla updated its FSD miles tracker, reflecting both a larger vehicle fleet and increased FSD usage. The fleet is now averaging 19.2 million miles per day on FSD — up from 14.4 million miles per day just a couple of months ago, representing approximately a 33% increase. Merritt noted this equates to 1,000 miles every 4.5 seconds. This accelerating data accumulation is a key input for model training velocity and a direct signal of FSD adoption growth, reinforcing the autonomous driving thesis.

3. **Robotaxi App Updated with Safety and Operational Features:** Tesla pushed an update to its Robotaxi app, adding a new tips section that informs riders how many seats are available, explains that vehicle lights will pulse upon arrival, and discloses that Tesla may use the interior cabin camera for safety monitoring. The app also received a darker visual appearance. Separately, Merritt flagged that Tesla has begun using cabin cameras to assess driver age — a feature he speculated could be used to prevent unaccompanied minors from hailing autonomous robotaxi rides. Together, these updates suggest Tesla is actively refining the operational and safety infrastructure for its robotaxi service ahead of broader deployment.

4. **Model Y Tops China Sales Charts in March 2026; New Market Launches:** The Tesla Model Y was the top-selling passenger vehicle in China in March 2026, with 39,827 retail registrations — beating all EVs and ICE models across sedans, SUVs, and MPVs. Merritt highlighted it was the only premium-priced model in the top ten, underscoring its competitive positioning. On the product front, Tesla officially launched the larger Model Y L in Israel, with first deliveries starting in June. Tesla also discontinued the white interior on all Model Y Premium trims built at Giga Shanghai (affecting Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, Japan, Philippines, and other markets), replacing it with a new Zen Grey interior. South Korea saw a 7.7% price increase on the Model Y L.

5. **Tesla Semi Factory on the Cusp of First Assembly Production:** A full factory tour of the Tesla Semi facility revealed a quote from Tesla's Dan Priestley: "We're right on the cusp of starting to produce first assemblies off these lines." This suggests Semi production is imminent, though no specific production date or volume target was stated.

---

## Signal Strength: **Strongly Bullish** — The Netherlands FSD approval is a structural regulatory breakthrough that opens the door to the broader European market, while surging FSD mileage and Robotaxi app refinements reinforce near-term autonomous deployment momentum.

2026-04-12.title: Elon Doesn't Compete. He Overwhelms. Here's How.
2026-04-12.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" argues that Elon Musk's competitive advantage across all his businesses — Tesla, SpaceX, xAI, and others — follows a single two-part playbook: build at a scale so large that unit economics favor him over all competitors, then iterate so fast that competitors can't catch up even if they wanted to. The host uses recent announcements, particularly xAI's Colossus 2 training seven AI models simultaneously, as a jumping-off point to trace this pattern across AI compute, Optimus, Cybercab, the car business, SpaceX, and Tesla's energy segment. The core investment thesis is that Tesla's stock price does not yet reflect the value of the scale infrastructure being built underneath each of these businesses.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Tesla's data flywheel vs. Waymo:** Tesla has over 7 million vehicles on the road globally, each equipped with eight cameras, and has logged over 9 billion miles of FSD driving data. Waymo, by contrast, operates a few thousand vehicles in a handful of cities and has driven approximately 170 million rider-only miles. The host frames this as a fundamental structural advantage: the larger the fleet, the faster the AI encounters new edge cases, learns from them, and improves. The host notes that Tesla added a billion FSD miles in just the first 50 days of 2026.

2. **Speed of AI improvement through scale:** Because Tesla's FSD AI is trained on data flowing from millions of vehicles simultaneously, each software update improves the entire fleet at once. The host argues this creates a self-reinforcing loop — more vehicles generate more data, which accelerates AI improvement, which enables safer driving, which unlocks regulatory approvals in more cities, which supports more vehicle deployment. The host acknowledges Waymo is further ahead today but argues Tesla is structurally positioned to scale much faster once Cybercab production begins.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab economics vs. Waymo:** The Cybercab is described as a purpose-built robotaxi with no steering wheel, no pedals, priced under $30,000 per unit, and targeting an operating cost of under $0.20 per mile at scale. Waymo vehicles are cited as costing over $200,000 each with all ride-hailing equipment included. The host argues this price gap makes it structurally impossible for Waymo to scale to millions of units, while Tesla can. The host flags the Cybercab production ramp as the key near-term catalyst to watch — specifically whether the unboxed manufacturing process works at Tesla's target scale.

2. **Self-reinforcing robotaxi growth loop:** The host describes a compounding loop specific to the robotaxi business: more Cybercab units generate more ride revenue and more driving data, which makes the fleet's AI smarter, which leads to safer driving, which leads to more city approvals, which supports more unit deployment. The host presents this as the most powerful expression of Tesla's scale-and-speed strategy.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus production targets vs. Boston Dynamics:** Tesla's stated target is 1 million Optimus robots per year from the Fremont factory, eventually scaling to 10 million per year from Giga Texas, at a unit cost of approximately $20,000–$30,000 each. Boston Dynamics, by comparison, has a factory capable of producing approximately 30,000 Atlas robots per year at a price above $140,000 each. The host frames this as Tesla targeting 33 times the volume at roughly one-fifth the price.

2. **Data advantage at robot scale:** The host argues that when Optimus robots run the same underlying AI as Tesla's vehicles, data from every robot working a factory shift feeds back into software improvements that are then pushed to the entire fleet simultaneously. At 30,000 units per year, design cycle validation is slow; at 1 million units per year, the learning speed is categorically different. The host identifies drone footage of Fremont's SNX lines being replaced by robot production equipment as the visual proof point to watch for confirming the million-unit target is real.

3. **Terafab chip manufacturing:** The $2 billion Terafab chip factory, which Intel has joined, targets 1 terawatt of AI compute per year — described as roughly 70% of TSMC's entire current global output from a single facility. The key speed advantage is that bringing photomask manufacturing in-house allows Tesla to design, build, test, and redesign chips in days rather than the months required when outsourcing to TSMC. Elon Musk estimated this enables 10x faster iteration on chip designs compared to competitors waiting in TSMC's queue.

## Energy
1. **Megapack deployment scale and margins:** Tesla deployed 46.7 gigawatt-hours of energy storage in 2025, up 48% year-over-year. Energy segment revenue reached $12.7 billion with gross margins of approximately 30%, making it Tesla's most profitable segment by margin. The host presents this as an underappreciated part of the Tesla thesis.

2. **Rapid factory expansion:** Tesla's Lathrop, California Megapack factory is already operational. The Shanghai Megapack factory started production in February 2025 with 40 gigawatt-hours of annual capacity. A Houston Megapack factory is coming online later in 2026 with an additional 50 gigawatt-hours of capacity. Once Houston is online, Tesla's total Megapack production capacity reaches approximately 133 gigawatt-hours per year — compared to total global energy storage deployment of approximately 92 gigawatt-hours in 2025. The host notes Tesla builds these factories in roughly one year versus the 2–3 years typical for competitors.

3. **Competitive position in energy storage:** The host cites Sungrow as holding approximately 14% global market share versus Tesla's approximately 15%, with BYD growing fast in China and Fluence carrying a $5.3 billion backlog. However, the host argues Tesla's vertical integration — controlling cells, pack design, software, and manufacturing in-house — gives it a compounding cost advantage over competitors who must source cells from CATL or LG.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Factory as the product:** The host reframes Tesla's EV advantage as residing in manufacturing capability, not the car itself. Tesla operates gigafactories on three continents — Fremont, Giga Texas, Giga Shanghai, and Giga Berlin — with combined capacity of approximately 2.5 million vehicles per year. Each factory is designed as a single integrated machine. The 4680 battery cell became Tesla's lowest-cost cell per kilowatt-hour by end of 2024, and the dry electrode process is expected to push costs another 30% lower.

2. **Factory build speed advantage:** Giga Shanghai went from an empty field to producing cars in under one year. Traditional automakers typically take three to five years to build a new factory. The host frames this speed of factory deployment as a strategic weapon — enabling Tesla to respond to demand shifts and enter new markets faster than any competitor.

3. **Competitor struggles at scale:** Rivian is cited as delivering approximately 50,000 vehicles in 2025 while burning billions. Lucid is described as running its single factory well under capacity. Ford's EV division is cited as having lost $15.5 billion in cumulative free cash flow. The host quotes an unnamed analyst describing manufacturing at Tesla's level as "insane mode hard."

4. **Cybercab unboxed manufacturing:** The Cybercab's unboxed manufacturing process is described as targeting a 40% reduction in factory footprint, 30% reduction in labor cost, and 50% reduction in assembly time, with a target cycle time of one unit every 10 seconds.

## Financials
1. **2026 capex commitment:** Tesla is planning to spend $20 billion in capital expenditure in 2026. The host flags this as a real risk — if robotaxi doesn't scale, if Optimus doesn't work, or if Terafab hits delays, that cash does not return. The host acknowledges scale magnifies losses as much as it magnifies wins.

2. **Elon's timeline track record:** The host offers a fair pushback that Elon Musk's execution timelines are consistently slower than promised — citing robotaxi promises dating to 2020, Optimus factory deployment, and Cybercab arriving later than originally stated. The host's framing: the risk of betting on Elon is timing; the risk of betting against him is direction.

## Market & Competition
1. **xAI Colossus 2 — parallel model training:** xAI is training seven AI models simultaneously on Colossus 2, including an image/video generator, two 1-trillion-parameter models, two 1.5-trillion-parameter models, one 6-trillion-parameter model, and one 10-trillion-parameter model. Each model trains in two to five weeks. The host contrasts this with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, which run one large training run at a time. Colossus 1 had 230,000 GPUs; Colossus 2 has over 550,000 GPUs running on 1 gigawatt of power, upgrading to 1.5 gigawatts in April 2026.

2. **SpaceX launch cadence as the proven template:** In 2025, SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions, representing 85% of all US orbital flights that year. Falcon 9's cost to orbit is approximately $2,700 per kilogram, the cheapest in the industry. Starship, once fully reusable, targets $100–$200 per kilogram — a 10–20x cost reduction. Blue Origin's New Glenn costs approximately $1,500 per kilogram; Rocket Lab's Neutron approximately $3,800 per kilogram. SpaceX has landed boosters over 400 times. Blue Origin flew New Glenn for the first time in January 2025 — one launch versus SpaceX's 165 that year.

Notable quotes and data:
- xAI training 7 models simultaneously on Colossus 2, including a 10-trillion-parameter model
- Colossus 1: 230,000 GPUs; Colossus 2: 550,000+ GPUs; power: 1 GW upgrading to 1.5 GW in April 2026
- Each xAI model trains in 2–5 weeks
- Tesla: 9 billion miles of FSD data; added 1 billion miles in the first 50 days of 2026
- Waymo: ~170 million rider-only miles; a few thousand vehicles in a handful of cities
- Optimus target: 1 million units/year at Fremont; 10 million/year eventually at Giga Texas; $20,000–$30,000 per unit
- Boston Dynamics Atlas: ~30,000 units/year capacity; price above $140,000 each
- Terafab: $2 billion facility, Intel as partner, targeting ~1 terawatt AI compute/year; Elon estimated 10x faster chip iteration
- Cybercab: under $30,000/unit; operating cost target under $0.20/mile; unboxed process cuts footprint 40%, labor 30%, assembly time 50%; target cycle time 1 unit per 10 seconds
- Tesla gigafactory combined capacity: ~2.5 million vehicles/year
- Giga Shanghai built in under 1 year (vs. 3–5 years industry standard)
- 4680 cells became lowest-cost cells per kWh by end of 2024; dry electrode process expected to cut costs another 30%
- Tesla energy: 46.7 GWh deployed in 2025 (+48% YoY); $12.7B revenue; ~30% gross margins
- Shanghai Megapack factory: online February 2025, 40 GWh annual capacity
- Houston Megapack factory: coming online later in 2026, 50 GWh capacity
- Tesla total Megapack capacity once Houston online: ~133 GWh/year vs. ~92 GWh global market deployment in 2025
- Tesla energy market share: ~15%; Sungrow: ~14%; Fluence backlog: $5.3 billion
- Ford EV division: $15.5 billion cumulative free cash flow loss
- Rivian: ~50,000 vehicles delivered in 2025
- SpaceX: 165 Falcon 9 launches in 2025 (85% of all US orbital flights); 400+ booster landings; $2,700/kg to orbit
- Starship target: $100–$200/kg to orbit
- Tesla 2026 capex plan: $20 billion
- "The factory is the product." — Elon Musk (as cited by host)
- "Scale isn't just a strategy for Elon. It's the strategy."

2026-04-12.title: Tesla Semi Faces A Brutal New Reality | OEVA 2026
2026-04-12.body:
This video is a recorded presentation by Brian, host of the YouTube channel Futurazza, delivered at the Oregon Electric Vehicle Association (OEVA) 2026 event, hosted at a Daimler facility. The talk focuses on the Freightliner eCascadia — a Class 8 electric semi-truck — covering its specs, history, economics, and competitive positioning, with a direct comparison to the Tesla Semi. The core argument is that while Tesla's Semi holds long-term promise, the eCascadia is the practical, available option today, and the Tesla Semi's limited availability and production delays make it largely a theoretical competitor for most fleet operators right now.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **eCascadia Overview and History:** The Freightliner eCascadia is an electrified version of the Cascadia platform introduced in 2007, a Class 8 truck rated for 80,000 lbs gross vehicle weight (with a regulatory allowance up to 82,000 lbs for electric vehicles). Freightliner began pilot production in 2019 with initial deployments at the Port of Long Beach and Penske Trucking in California. By 2020 they had dozens of units with various customers, by 2021 over 100 units, by 2022 they were in serial (though low-volume) production with 100 different customers, and by 2025, Schneider alone had 100 trucks logging 10 million miles — averaging over 100,000 miles per truck.

2. **Performance Specs — Torque and Power:** The eCascadia is available in single-axle and tandem-axle configurations. Horsepower ranges from approximately 320 to 470 hp depending on configuration, but the vehicle's primary performance advantage lies in torque: 11,500 lb-ft for the single-axle and 23,000 lb-ft for the tandem axle. Attendees noted that comparable diesel engines produce roughly 3,000 lb-ft of torque. The electric drivetrain enables the truck to climb grades without gearing down, and regenerative braking recovers energy on descents — reducing brake dust, eliminating engine braking noise (Jake brakes), and improving net energy efficiency.

3. **Battery and Range:** Battery capacity ranges from 291 kWh to 438 kWh depending on configuration, yielding an estimated range of approximately 150 to 230 miles. The battery chemistry is NMC (nickel manganese cobalt), supplied by CATL (referred to in the transcript as "CL") from China. The presenter noted the battery is subject to a 25% tariff, and while a tariff drawback might exist given sales volumes, he could not confirm it. He speculated battery life could reach approximately 500,000 miles, though range degradation — particularly from frequent 100% charging — remains a concern. The eCascadia only comes in a day cab configuration (no sleeper option in the electric version, unlike the diesel Cascadia).

4. **Charging Infrastructure and Speed:** Because the eCascadia entered pilot production in 2019, it was built around the CCS1 charging standard — the only standard available for trucks at the time. A single CCS1 handle delivers approximately 180 kW; using two handles simultaneously can reach 270–280 kW, achieving a 10–80% charge in approximately 90 minutes. A joint public charging venture was established with NextEra and BlackRock under the brand "Green Lane," including a major site in Colton, California featuring over 40 chargers, solar canopy, and pull-through lanes. Green Lane has plans to add MCS (Megawatt Charging System) connectors to that site and is scouting additional MCS-capable locations. Faster charging is planned for the next vehicle program, timeline unspecified. A representative noted transformer supply constraints in the U.S. remain a limiting factor for faster charging infrastructure deployment, though transformer production is ramping in other markets.

5. **Weight Advantage Over Tesla Semi:** The eCascadia weighs between 16,500 and 21,800 lbs (curb weight depending on configuration), which is approximately 3,000 lbs lighter than the Tesla Semi in each comparable configuration. Combined with the 82,000 lb GVWR allowance for electric trucks, this means fleet operators can carry 2,000–3,000 lbs more payload with the eCascadia than with either a Tesla Semi or a diesel truck.

6. **Pricing and Total Cost of Ownership:** The eCascadia does not have a publicly listed price. Industry-wide, the average Class 8 electric truck cost approximately $411,000 in 2025. Estimates for the eCascadia range from $400,000 to $500,000, compared to a diesel Cascadia priced at roughly $120,000 (day cab) to $180,000 (sleeper). A Canadian study found operators can save approximately $167,000–$170,000 in fuel and maintenance over six years compared to a diesel Cascadia. Available incentives include up to $185,000 in New York and $120,000–$150,000 in California (with higher amounts for drayage trucks). With incentives, the presenter suggested total cost of ownership approaches parity after roughly seven to eight years. He estimated that a price point around $300,000 would be needed for the eCascadia to compete effectively without heavy reliance on incentives.

7. **Domestic Battery Production Plans:** Freightliner is working to domesticate battery production through a joint venture in Mississippi with Cummins, PACCAR, and Freightliner. This would eliminate the 25% tariff on imported CATL cells, reduce shipping costs and lead times, and qualify for battery manufacturing incentives at multiple levels. Domestic batteries from this venture are expected around 2027.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla Semi's Real-World Availability:** Brian directly challenged the assumption that the Tesla Semi is a competitive alternative today, noting that very few customers have actually received trucks. He referenced early California grant applications suggesting Tesla Semi pricing in the $240,000–$260,000 range, but cautioned these could be loss leaders and that Tesla has significant capex to depreciate. He acknowledged Tesla's strategy of high volume and lower pricing but questioned whether that scale would materialize. The eCascadia's key advantage today is simply that it exists, can be purchased, and fits into existing Cascadia-based fleet operations.

2. **Fleet Integration Advantage:** For fleets already running diesel Cascadias, the eCascadia offers a parts and service compatibility advantage — a high percentage of frame, cab, and structural components are shared, meaning fleet operators maintain one parts inventory and can leverage Freightliner's well-established nationwide service center network. An attendee from a school district illustrated the challenge of maintaining two separate parts streams for mixed fleets, underscoring the practical value of platform continuity.

3. **Competitive Landscape and China:** The presenter acknowledged that ground-up, purpose-built electric trucks — as Chinese manufacturers and Tesla are producing — will ultimately be cheaper than platform-adapted designs. However, he argued that the eCascadia's earlier market entry built important manufacturing and operational competencies, and that Freightliner likely has a next-generation purpose-built electric truck in development. The broader industry inflection point, he argued, will come when electric truck pricing drops to the point where the payback period is short enough — ideally well under 10 years — to make diesel obsolete without relying on government incentives.

Notable quotes and data:
- eCascadia GVWR: 82,000 lbs (vs. 80,000 lbs for diesel)
- Torque: 11,500 lb-ft (single axle), 23,000 lb-ft (tandem axle)
- Battery: 291 kWh to 438 kWh; NMC chemistry from CATL
- Range: approximately 150–230 miles depending on configuration
- Charging: up to ~280 kW with dual CCS1 handles; 10–80% in ~90 minutes
- Curb weight: 16,500–21,800 lbs (approximately 3,000 lbs lighter than Tesla Semi)
- Industry average Class 8 EV price (2025): $411,000
- eCascadia estimated price: $400,000–$500,000
- Diesel Cascadia: $120,000 (day cab), $180,000 (sleeper)
- Fuel and maintenance savings vs. diesel: ~$167,000–$170,000 over 6 years
- Incentives: up to $185,000 (New York), $120,000–$150,000 (California)
- Price target for diesel parity without incentives: ~$300,000
- Tesla Semi early grant pricing estimates: ~$240,000–$260,000 (unconfirmed, possibly loss leaders)
- Schneider fleet (as of 2025): 100 trucks, 10 million miles logged
- Green Lane charging site (Colton, CA): 40+ chargers, solar canopy, pull-through lanes; MCS addition planned
- Battery joint venture domestic production: Mississippi, with Cummins, PACCAR, Freightliner; expected ~2027
- *"If the price gets low enough, it's over for diesel."*
- *"If you want to know who's ahead today, it's the people who actually have a truck you can buy."*

2026-04-12.title: Daily X Summary (2026-04-12)
2026-04-12.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts centered on two meaningful developments: Tesla's geographic expansion of FSD (Supervised) into the Netherlands (a new European market), and continued Cybercab validation testing spreading to new U.S. locations. A secondary story is Tesla's announcement of limited-edition farewell variants of the Model S and Model X, signaling the wind-down of those vehicle lines.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD (Supervised) Launches in the Netherlands:** In two posts (garnering a combined ~5.9K likes and 509 reposts), Sawyer Merritt reported that Tesla FSD (Supervised) is officially rolling out to customer vehicles in the Netherlands — marking a notable European market expansion. Notably, Tesla is requiring all Dutch owners activating FSD for the first time to complete a short educational quiz confirming they understand how the system operates before it engages. Tesla published a dedicated video explaining FSD's functionality for this rollout. This appears to be the first confirmed European retail customer deployment of FSD (Supervised), representing a regulatory and geographic milestone.

2. **Cybercab Validation Testing Expands to Kansas:** A post with 2.6K likes and 242 reposts flagged a Cybercab spotted testing in Wichita, Kansas — described as the first time a Cybercab has been seen in that state. Merritt noted that Tesla has recently produced significantly more engineering and validation Cybercabs, and suggested investors should expect sightings in many new geographic areas as the validation program broadens. This is consistent with a pre-production engineering validation push ahead of a manufacturing ramp, and the geographic spread of testing units is a qualitative signal of program progress.

3. **Tesla Announces Signature Edition Model S and Model X as Final Farewell:** Tesla announced limited "Signature Edition" versions of the Model S and Model X, framed explicitly as a final goodbye for both vehicle lines. Priced at $159,420, only 250 Model S and 100 Model X units will be produced, all in Plaid configuration with a Garnet Red exterior paint and matching door handles. The strict production caps (350 total units) and the "farewell" framing confirm Tesla is formally retiring these two flagship sedans/SUVs, likely to redirect resources toward next-generation platforms.

4. **SpaceX Starlink Chip Development (Low Tesla Relevance):** Merritt noted a SpaceX job posting hinting at development of compact multi-chip modules for Starlink Mobile radio frequency handling. This has no direct Tesla investment relevance and is included only for completeness; it was skipped for deeper analysis.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — FSD's first European retail deployment and broadening Cybercab validation testing are incremental positive catalysts for the autonomous driving thesis, while the Model S/X retirement signals continued portfolio rationalization toward higher-margin next-gen vehicles.

2026-04-13.title: Tesla Stock Might Not Be What It Looks Like
2026-04-13.body:
This video features host Herbert interviewing Larry Goldberg, a serial entrepreneur and venture capitalist, in a wide-ranging discussion about whether Tesla stock is undervalued, overvalued, or fairly priced at its current mid-$300s level. The central thesis is that Tesla's valuation depends entirely on which version of the company you're evaluating — the struggling car business suggests overvaluation, while the broader portfolio of robotaxi, Optimus, AI, and energy suggests significant undervaluation relative to future potential. Both the bull and bear cases are presented as simultaneously valid depending on the investor's time horizon.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Auto Business Decline Driving Bear Case:** Tesla's car business is the primary basis for the bear argument. Earnings dropped 47% in the prior year, deliveries are flat, and the auto segment revenue is cited as having moved from negative $9 billion to $18 billion over a multi-year period. Bears argue that judged purely as an automaker, Tesla stock at mid-$300s is significantly overvalued, with some suggesting a fair value closer to $50–$100 for a pure auto company. Elon Musk's earlier projection of 20 million vehicle sales per year was cited as another missed target.

2. **FSD Adoption Problem Among Existing Owners:** Larry Goldberg highlights what he calls a genuine failure — Tesla's inability to get its existing customer base to actually use Full Self-Driving. He notes that while he personally uses FSD approximately 98% of the time and his wife uses it 94–95% of the time, he observes fellow Tesla owners in the Research Triangle Park area gripping the steering wheel and driving manually, even when they own FSD. He sees this as a meaningful missed opportunity, though both he and the host believe adoption will accelerate as the technology becomes more demonstrably reliable.

3. **Technology Inflection Point for Consumer Adoption:** The host shares a personal anecdote about his sister — previously a Mercedes and BMW loyalist who had no interest in Tesla — deciding to purchase a Tesla after being driven around Vancouver, Canada in Full Self-Driving mode for hours without incident. The host frames this as evidence that FSD has crossed a threshold from beta testing to genuinely useful technology, which he believes will drive broader consumer adoption. He notes a newer FSD version is expected to push capabilities further.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD Going Global and Version Expectations:** The host references FSD going global as one of the key developments being tracked. A newer FSD version (referred to as FSD 14.3) is described as highly anticipated, with some interpreting delays in its arrival as meaning a promised 10x parameter improvement did not materialize on schedule. The host and guest remain confident the technology trajectory is intact, even if specific release timing is uncertain.

2. **Unsupervised FSD as a Solved Problem in Principle:** The host states his personal view that robotaxi and FSD are "solved" from a technology standpoint, framing remaining challenges as timing and scale rather than fundamental feasibility. He acknowledges unsupervised deployment will take more time to fully roll out across cities, but argues the technology is no longer in question, pointing to ongoing hiring activity as evidence of continued expansion plans.

## Robotaxi
1. **Austin Robotaxi Launch Referenced:** The host mentions robotaxi deployment in Austin as an active near-term development, citing it alongside FSD going global and Cybercab production starting as key catalysts. No specific launch date or fleet size is provided beyond the general reference to Austin being the initial deployment city.

2. **Cybercab Production Starting:** The host states that Cybercab production is starting "this month" (relative to the video's April 2026 publish date), framing it as one of the key bullish near-term catalysts alongside the Austin robotaxi launch. No specific production volume or ramp rate is mentioned in this context.

3. **Missed Robotaxi Timeline History:** The host catalogs a series of missed robotaxi timelines from Elon Musk: a claim in 2020 of 1 million robotaxis "next year," a statement that 50% of the US would have robotaxi service by a certain date that passed without fulfillment, and a more recent projection of robotaxi expanding to many cities by year-end 2025 that was pushed to mid-2026. These are presented not as disqualifying but as consistent with Elon's pattern of aspirational target-setting.

4. **Ark Invest $2,900 Price Target for 2029–2030:** The host references Ark Invest's published price target of $2,900 per share by 2029–2030. A separate analyst referred to as "Cern" is cited as having conducted a sum-of-the-parts valuation, discounting future segment values back to present value with a 50% probability haircut applied conservatively, and arriving at a present value still above $3,000 per share — suggesting even the discounted bull case implies the current ~$350 price has not priced in most of the upside.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus Production Line Announced at Fremont:** The host states that Tesla has announced a 1 million units per year Optimus production line being built at Fremont, and that this can now be physically observed happening in an actual factory. He frames this as a meaningful shift from speculation to observable construction progress. A separate 10 million units per year production line is referenced as being built at Giga Texas.

2. **Optimus Timeline Slippage:** The host notes that Elon's earlier projection of 5,000–10,000 Optimus units by end of 2025 was not achieved, with production start now pushed to 2026. This is grouped with other missed timelines but not treated as a sign the project is at risk — the host explicitly states Optimus has not been shelved and that progress is visible.

## Energy
1. **Energy Segment Financial Performance:** The energy business is cited as generating $12.7 billion in revenue with approximately 30% margins, presented as one of the strongest performing segments and a key part of the bull case. The host and guest note that energy is still in relatively early stages, currently focused on conventional battery storage and solar systems, but frame it as having enormous future potential — particularly in the context of a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger and AI-driven energy demand.

2. **Energy as a Long-Term Strategic Asset:** Larry Goldberg argues that energy will become "the currency of the future" and that the opportunities in energy are gigantic, especially when considered alongside a potential SpaceX partnership or merger. He suggests the market has not yet begun to appreciate the full scale of Tesla's energy opportunity, framing current deployments as foundational infrastructure for something much larger.

## Financials
1. **Tesla Financial Metrics Q1 2021 vs. Q4 2025 Comparison:** The host presents a comparison showing Tesla's growth over roughly five years: GAAP income grew from $438 million to approximately $840 million (roughly doubled), auto revenue grew from negative $9 billion to $18 billion, and energy revenue reached close to $4 billion. These figures are used to argue that Tesla the business has substantially improved even as the stock price has remained relatively flat over the same period, making the current valuation appear more reasonable than the 2021 peak.

2. **Capital Expenditure Trajectory:** Larry Goldberg references a prior projection he made about Tesla's capital consumption rate, noting he was approximately one to one and a half years ahead of where the company actually landed, and projecting Tesla will reach approximately $40 billion per year in capital spend. He notes that xAI and SpaceX have absorbed some capital deployment that might otherwise have gone through Tesla, and argues a potential merger of Tesla and SpaceX would create a combined entity with over $110 billion in capital resources.

3. **Valuation Framework — PE Ratio Criticism:** The video references analyst Alex Voit's argument that using the P/E ratio to evaluate Tesla is a mistake appropriate only for pure-play automakers, not for growth companies with multiple emerging business lines. Larry Goldberg echoes this by drawing a parallel to Nvidia in 2022, arguing that anyone using conventional valuation metrics to dismiss Tesla's stock price-to-sales ratio is making the same error made by those who dismissed Nvidia before its breakout.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX Merger Speculation as Long-Term Catalyst:** Larry Goldberg repeatedly references the prospect of a Tesla-SpaceX merger as a potential transformational event, arguing it would combine Tesla's ~$40 billion capital spend with SpaceX's ~$75 billion to create a company with over $110 billion in combined capital, deployed with what he describes as Elon's uniquely capital-efficient execution style. He compares xAI's rapid rise to frontier AI status at a fraction of OpenAI's or Anthropic's spend as evidence of this capital efficiency.

2. **Bear vs. Bull Framing as a Time Horizon Question:** Both the host and Larry Goldberg converge on the view that Tesla bears and bulls can simultaneously be correct — bears who expect further near-term stock weakness are not wrong given the lack of near-term earnings catalysts, while long-term bulls remain correct if any one of the multiple major business opportunities (robotaxi, Optimus, AI, energy) materializes. The host explicitly frames his investment thesis as a bet on product and business progress rather than near-term price prediction.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla stock down over 20% since start of 2026, trading in mid-$300s at time of recording
- Earnings dropped 47% in the prior year
- Energy segment: $12.7 billion revenue at ~30% margins
- Q1 2021 to Q4 2025: GAAP income $438M → ~$840M; auto revenue $9B → $18B; energy revenue ~$4B
- Ark Invest price target: $2,900 by 2029–2030
- "Cern" sum-of-the-parts present value estimate: above $3,000 per share even with 50% probability discount
- Optimus production line at Fremont: 1 million units/year capacity announced; 10 million units/year line under construction at Giga Texas
- Projected combined Tesla + SpaceX capital: ~$110 billion+ annually
- Tesla projected capex: ~$40 billion/year
- Larry Goldberg: "I can easily find $1,000, $2,000 in the stock price on multiple different futures."
- Larry Goldberg: "I accept that the date is going to go out. I take the goal, but I don't accept the date."
- Host: "Has anything happened in the last 3 months that has shown you that none of these products and businesses are now not going to happen anymore? My answer is still no."

2026-04-13.title: Tesla Europe Breakthrough Just Changed Everything This Weekend
2026-04-13.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel covers Tesla's landmark approval of FSD Supervised in the Netherlands and the immediate push by Dutch regulators to seek EU-wide approval, which the host and guest Jeff (a multi-decade supply chain executive and manufacturing consultant) argue is a pivotal moment for Tesla's global autonomous driving expansion. The core thesis is that the Netherlands approval is not just a single-country win but a gateway to broader European and international FSD adoption, laying critical groundwork for the eventual robotaxi rollout. The video also covers ongoing robotaxi hiring in Texas, a new Optimus charging job posting, and two recently rolled-out vehicle software features.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Netherlands FSD Supervised Approval — First in Europe:** Tesla's FSD Supervised received regulatory approval in the Netherlands from the RDW (Dutch Vehicle Authority) for the first time in Europe. The host notes that the RDW conducted 18 months of rigorous testing and concluded that FSD would make roads net safer. Elon Musk publicly congratulated the team and acknowledged the regulators were "extremely rigorous" in their review. The version approved in Europe is designated 2026.3.6 in local naming conventions, but Elon confirmed it is the equivalent of FSD version 14.3.

2. **Push for EU-Wide Approval:** The general manager of the RDW announced just two days after the Netherlands approval that the Dutch Vehicle Authority plans to notify the European Commission and seek EU-wide approval for Tesla's FSD Supervised. A majority vote among responsible EU member states is required for approval to pass. The host and guest note that the RDW is widely recognized as a standard-setter that influences almost all of Europe, and that approval could extend beyond the 27 EU member states to additional countries that follow European regulation — a point confirmed by Ashok Elluswami on X.

3. **Timeline for Broader European Approvals:** Jeff estimates that additional country approvals could begin flowing in within the next 4 to 8 weeks, with end of summer as a worst-case scenario. He emphasizes that no additional hardware is required — existing Tesla vehicles in Europe already have the necessary hardware and only need a software update. Tesla has also already sent customers a tutorial via email and embedded one in the vehicle software, which must be played before FSD can be used.

4. **FSD Performance in European Conditions:** Early customer videos from the Netherlands, including footage in Amsterdam city center, showed FSD navigating narrow roads, heavy cyclist and pedestrian traffic, roundabouts, and road works. Elon confirmed that Tesla's self-driving handles Dutch roundabouts well. Jeff highlighted that FSD version 14.3 has significantly faster reaction times than prior versions, as documented in Tesla's own release notes, and compared the system's eight-camera 360-degree coverage favorably to the limitations of human vision.

5. **Cross-Border Warnings and European-Specific UI Features:** When crossing into a country where FSD is not yet approved, drivers receive a 15-second advance warning to take over. The host noted that European FSD also includes a mandatory video tutorial before first use and a more detailed FSD usage tracking UI — features the host described as potentially ahead of the US experience. He drew a parallel to how similar state-border warnings may function in the US once unsupervised FSD is approved in some states but not others.

6. **Global Regulatory Ripple Effect:** Jeff argued that Europe's approval — from one of the world's toughest regulatory environments — will encourage other countries to either conduct their own testing with a higher degree of confidence or simply accept the European approval report as sufficient. Ashok noted that European regulation is followed by many more countries beyond the 27 EU member states. The host also flagged China as the next major expected approval, noting there are over a million Tesla vehicles already in China.

7. **Safety Data and the Path to Unsupervised FSD:** The guest referenced nearly 10 billion miles of FSD data captured, particularly on more recent releases, as evidence that the system is many times safer than human driving. He framed the European supervised approval as the essential foundation for eventually obtaining unmanned/unsupervised approvals in Europe and globally, arguing that regulators who have seen FSD perform well in supervised mode will be more receptive to future unsupervised applications.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi Field Response Specialist Hiring Ramp in Texas:** Tesla is actively ramping up hiring of robotaxi field response specialists across Austin, Houston, and Dallas, Texas, with day, afternoon, and night shifts being filled. The job involves immediate on-road support for autonomous vehicle incidents, ensuring rider safety, conducting basic roadside repairs, assisting first responders, and aiding vehicle recovery. The host argued this hiring pattern is consistent with an imminent commercial robotaxi service launch, not merely expanded testing.

2. **Debate Over Robotaxi Launch Readiness:** Jeff acknowledged that milestones discussed at the end of January 2026 (including doubling deployments every month) have not been met, but pushed back on narratives linking the delay to a requirement for FSD version 15. He argued the pace of job postings does not suggest a slowdown and that Tesla is likely between two software releases while validating safety performance. Both host and guest expressed a desire to see new supervised robotaxi cities launched this month (April 2026), with concern that remaining at just Austin and the Bay Area through the end of April would be a negative signal.

3. **Pre-Earnings Robotaxi and Cybercab Announcements Anticipated:** The guest suggested Tesla may time a new city rollout or a Cybercab production start announcement prior to the April 22, 2026 earnings call to give management positive milestones to discuss. He noted that analysts will likely press management on why the January 29th guidance of doubling deployments monthly has not been achieved and what is different now. The host speculated that Giga Berlin — following the union's recent loss — could potentially be announced as a Cybercab and Optimus production site, given Elon's earlier comments about making it Europe's largest factory.

4. **Long-Term Vision: Automation of Field Response:** Jeff noted that while Tesla is hiring significant numbers of human field response staff now, the long-term expectation is that these manual processes will be progressively automated using AI, with human staffing scaled to satisfy regulatory and local government requirements during the transition period.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Charging Infrastructure Hiring:** Tesla posted a senior software engineer role for residential vehicle and robot charging, with the role explicitly covering the "full stack of Tesla's home charging and human robot charging products," including the universal mobile connector, wall connector, and Optimus charging. Jeff noted this points toward a unified Tesla app experience integrating car charging, home energy (Powerwall), and Optimus robot charging under a single interface.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **European Tesla Fleet Size and FSD Monetization Opportunity:** The host estimated there are approximately 1.2 million Tesla vehicles sold in Europe over the last 5 to 6 years that are now eligible for FSD via software update. He and Jeff framed this as a significant incremental revenue opportunity from FSD subscriptions. The European FSD subscription is priced at €99 per month, and a one-time purchase option also appears to be available in the European market.

## Financials

1. **April 22, 2026 Earnings Call — Key Questions:** The guest flagged several open questions for the upcoming April 22, 2026 earnings call: whether Tesla will change or hold its robotaxi rollout guidance from the January 29th call, what happened in the energy segment (described as a "big drop off from expectations"), and whether the company was supply-constrained in energy or facing typical lumpiness. He also noted that FSD version 14.3 going wide and new city launches before the call would meaningfully improve the tone of the earnings discussion.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk: "It's like getting an iPhone after only using flip phones" — on Europeans experiencing FSD version 14.3 after basic Autopilot highway lane assist.
- Jeff: "If you remember three things from this whole approval in Europe: one is RDW is the gateway to the rest of the 27 EU member states; two, they tested it rigorously for 18 months and said it's very good and will make roads net safer; three, the general manager immediately said they're going to push for EU-wide approval."
- Ashok Elluswami: "The European regulation is followed by a lot more countries than just the ones in the EU."
- FSD Europe subscription price: €99/month; one-time purchase option also listed.
- Approximately 1.2 million Tesla vehicles sold in Europe over the last ~5–6 years, all eligible for FSD via OTA update.
- Tesla FSD has captured nearly 10 billion miles of data, particularly on recent releases.
- FSD version in Europe: locally named 2026.3.6, confirmed by Elon to be the equivalent of version 14.3.
- RDW testing period for FSD: 18 months of rigorous evaluation.
- April 22, 2026: Tesla earnings call date.
