The hosts express hope the trial resolves quickly and does not become a significant distraction for Elon, whose primary focus they characterize as autonomy at scale, humanoid bots, Starship, and XAI/Grok 5.

3. **SpaceX Acquires Rights to Buy Cursor for $60 Billion:** SpaceX struck a deal giving it the right to acquire Cursor — an AI coding platform — for $60 billion later in 2026. If SpaceX does not exercise that option, it pays Cursor $10 billion to continue the partnership. The strategic rationale is that XAI currently lags Anthropic and OpenAI in coding and agentic AI workflows; Cursor would give XAI access to a leading coding interface and agentic tooling. In return, Cursor gains access to XAI's Colossus and Colossus 2 data centers, which are described as the largest and most coherent supercomputers in the world — infrastructure that both Anthropic and OpenAI are currently constrained on, with Anthropic reportedly relying on ASICs rather than Nvidia H100s.

4. **Nvidia's Awkward Position with Cursor:** The hosts discuss a media narrative that SpaceX's Cursor deal puts Nvidia in an uncomfortable spot, since Nvidia engineers are heavy Cursor users and Nvidia is also an investor in the platform. The concern raised in the press is that companies may hesitate to embed critical workflows in software controlled by a direct competitor like Elon. The hosts largely dismiss this concern, noting that Elon and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have mutual respect and will likely work it out. They also note that Sam Altman publicly emailed Jensen Huang about using OpenAI's Codex (their competing coding tool) across Nvidia instead, with Huang responding positively.

5. **XAI's Competitive Position in AI Coding:** The hosts acknowledge XAI is currently behind Anthropic and OpenAI in coding AI. Anthropic's Claude models have been dominant (Claude 4.6 was best-in-class for an extended period, with 4.7 rolling out since), while OpenAI's Codex has also been well-received. Both are described as entering recursive self-improvement loops in coding — using their own coding AIs to build more features — which could compound their leads exponentially. However, the hosts and a cited source (Larry Goldberg) argue this is "early innings" and that larger supercomputer infrastructure ultimately determines AI quality, which is XAI's long-term bet.

6. **AI Data Center Regulatory Headwinds:** The hosts flag that approximately 50% of AI data center projects in the US have been stalled or abandoned due to regulatory and legal pushback, though they note they could not recall the exact figure. This is described as a dangerous trend, as it concentrates data centers in the middle of the country rather than keeping them regionally dispersed. The hosts express concern that anti-AI sentiment is becoming a political platform and urge smarter regulatory frameworks rather than moratoriums, while also criticizing hyperbolic AI doom messaging from some AI CEOs as counterproductive.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Fremont Factory Converting to Optimus Production at 1 Million Units Per Year:** Tesla is actively converting its Fremont factory to produce Optimus humanoid robots, targeting a 1 million unit per year run rate. Jeff Lutz clarifies this is his own framing ("self-dubbed"), not an official Tesla designation, but reflects the scale of the buildout. He expects the Fremont production line to begin producing thousands of units in 2026, with the full million-unit run rate taking roughly a year to achieve after the line spins up.

2. **Giga Texas 10 Million Per Year Optimus Facility Breaking Ground:** Aerial photos from Joe Tegtmeyer show land near Giga Texas being prepared for a dedicated Optimus manufacturing facility targeting 10 million units per year. Jeff Lutz predicts the factory structure will be framed by end of 2026 and the factory itself will be ready in 2027. He cautions the facility will not hit 10 million units immediately upon opening — ramp-up will take a couple of years — but expresses hope the first Optimus bot could roll off that line by end of 2027.

3. **Optimus V3 Status — Engineering Units Exist, Public Demo Delayed:** Tesla has Optimus V3 units in-house and is doing engineering work on them, but is not showing them publicly. Jeff Lutz explains the delay as primarily technical: when introducing new hardware, new mechanics, and potentially new motors, the team needs significant tuning time to get V3 back to V2.5's capability level before surpassing it and doing a public demo. He expects the demo to be timed close to the start of production. Elon had previously indicated production start in July–August 2026, with Jeff noting July is approximately 90 days from the time of recording and that the timeline may land closer to September–October.

4. **No Other Company Committing to 1M and 10M Scale Buildouts:** The hosts challenge the narrative that Tesla is behind in humanoid robots by pointing out that no other company — including Chinese competitors currently selling tens of thousands of units — has committed to and begun building manufacturing facilities at the 1 million and 10 million unit per year scale. They argue the key signal is factory construction and proven volume manufacturing capability, not demo performance. They also highlight Tesla's recent earnings report, which included a $230 million warranty true-down, meaning Tesla vehicles failed at a lower rate and cost less to repair than previously estimated — evidence of the product quality discipline they expect to apply to Optimus.

## Autonomous Driving / Robotaxi

1. **Waymo Referenced as Current Robotaxi Benchmark:** The hosts briefly reference Waymo having approximately 3,000 vehicles operating in robotaxi service as the current benchmark for deployed autonomous vehicles, contrasting this with Tesla's not-yet-deployed robotaxi fleet. This is cited as an example of the broader pattern where Tesla appears behind on visible metrics while building toward a much larger scale deployment.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon is seeking **$130 billion** in remedies from OpenAI, which he has committed to returning to OpenAI's nonprofit.
- Elon's initial contribution to OpenAI was approximately **$150 million**, given to a nonprofit.
- SpaceX has the right to acquire Cursor for **$60 billion** later in 2026, or pay **$10 billion** if they don't.
- Waymo currently has approximately **3,000 vehicles** in robotaxi service.
- Tesla posted a **$230 million warranty true-down** in the most recent earnings, indicating vehicles failed at a lower rate and cost less to repair than modeled.
- Fremont Optimus target: **1 million units per year** run rate.
- Giga Texas Optimus facility target: **10 million units per year** run rate.
- Optimus V3 production start guided by Elon: **July–August 2026** (Jeff Lutz's estimate: may land September–October 2026).
- Approximately **50%** of AI data center projects in the US have been stalled or abandoned (hosts flagged this as an approximate figure they could not precisely verify).
- Jeff Lutz predicts: Giga Texas Optimus factory **framed by end of 2026**, producing first bots by **end of 2027**.
- *"Whatever they decide to build, whether it's agents or whatever, you're going to have access to it from your Optimus robot. You're going to have access to it in your Tesla vehicle."* — Jeff Lutz
- *"Elon once again he's playing the long game. He's vertically integrating."* — Jeff Lutz

2026-04-28.title: Tesla FSD 14.3.2 Is a Magnitude Leap Forward
2026-04-28.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi — an economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur — discussing the state of Tesla's Full Self-Driving technology, robotaxi deployment progress, and competitive positioning. The core thesis is that FSD's fundamental safety capability has effectively been solved, and the remaining challenges are operational infrastructure and scaling convenience — not core AI — and that no competitor is close to matching Tesla's real-world deployment infrastructure.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3.2 Rolling Out Wide with Dramatic Community Reception:** FSD version 14.3.2 is described as now going wide, with software update labeled 2026.2.9, and is reportedly being rolled out to all HW4 (AI4) models — marking the first wide rollout (defined as more than 5% of vehicles) after numerous prior releases. Community feedback is described as overwhelmingly positive, with users calling it a "magnitude leap" over version 14.3.1, despite the minor-seeming version number increment. Herbert emphasizes that the jump in quality is surprising given how small the version number change appears.

2. **FSD 14.3 as a Rearchitected Model:** Jo Bhakdi stresses that version 14.3 is not a routine incremental improvement but a deeply reworked, rearchitected model designed to allow much faster and deeper iterations going forward. He argues this architectural change means significant improvements should be expected with every subsequent iteration, and that the improvement curves are steepening — leading him to extrapolate that FSD will be effectively solved well before the end of 2026.

3. **Safety Highlighted by Tesla Executives — Proactive and Contextual Intelligence:** Multiple videos shared in the episode showcase FSD 14.3.2 demonstrating advanced situational awareness. In one clip, the car pulled onto the shoulder to avoid a fast-approaching vehicle making an unsignaled lane change, then re-entered traffic and yielded for a merging car — a sequence the driver initially found alarming but retrospectively praised. In another, FSD held back from advancing at an intersection and then reversed to make room for a wide-turning truck trailer, anticipating the swing before it happened. Tesla VP of AI Ashok Kaliswami described this as "the advantage of having eyes all around" and called it "big brain in a small box." Tesla AI executive Phil Dwan is quoted saying "safety is best when it's proactive."

4. **Safety vs. Convenience as the Core Engineering Tradeoff:** Jo Bhakdi articulates what he describes as a key insight from the earnings call: Tesla has deliberately prioritized safety over convenience, instructing the system to hesitate when in doubt. The result is a car that is sometimes inconveniently cautious — e.g., stopping at green lights too long or driving in circles — but this is a conscious design choice. The challenge now is using continued capability improvements to converge safety and convenience simultaneously, rather than sacrificing one for the other.

5. **Sweden Municipality Approves FSD Testing for One Year:** A small municipality in Sweden approved Tesla FSD testing on its road network for a one-year period. Herbert clarifies this is not final regulatory approval for autonomous operation, but a testing step. Jo Bhakdi contextualizes this within Sweden's decentralized governance structure, noting that diligent decisions by small Swedish communities tend to be adopted more broadly. He also expresses the broader view that regulatory approvals are secondary to technology readiness — once Tesla has tens of thousands of robotaxis operating in the U.S., regulators globally will fall in line quickly.

6. **Netherlands EU Approval Process Moving:** Herbert mentions that the Netherlands has a meeting scheduled for May 5th, with a potential EU member-state decision on FSD approval possible in late June 2026, if the process proceeds as planned.

## Robotaxi

1. **Current Cybercab Production Rate and Fleet Size:** Jo Bhakdi estimates the current Cybercab production rate at approximately 10–12 units per day, with roughly 640 robotaxis currently deployed. He projects this pace would yield approximately 300 per month now, scaling to potentially 10,000 by December 2026 if the ramp continues. Herbert's own estimate is 15,000 Cybercabs produced by end of 2026, with Jo noting there may be 20,000–25,000 produced but uncertainty about how many will be deployed in robotaxi service versus other uses by year-end.

2. **Elon's "Not Super Material" Comment Reinterpreted:** The hosts discuss Elon Musk's earnings call statement that robotaxi revenue would be "not super material" by end of 2026. Jo Bhakdi runs the math, estimating that even 2,000 annualized robotaxi-equivalent units would represent only about 5% of free cash flow — and with the fleet only reaching scale in the final months of the year, the annualized contribution would be closer to 1–2% of 2026 free cash flow. They argue this makes the "not material" statement mathematically consistent with producing 15,000–25,000 Cybercabs by December.

3. **Tesla's Strategy: Build for Million-Scale, Not Patch to 4,000:** Jo Bhakdi draws a sharp strategic contrast between Tesla and Waymo. Waymo, with approximately 3,000 cars across five cities and expanding to ten cities this year, is described as "patching its way" to incremental fleet growth — a 3,000 → 4,000 car strategy. Tesla, by contrast, is building systems and infrastructure intended to scale to millions of vehicles, which requires solving fundamentally different problems and cannot be rushed through incremental patching.

4. **Waymo Incident — Hit-and-Run Behavior After Multi-Car Accident:** The hosts play a video showing a Waymo vehicle that, after being rear-ended, appeared to leave the scene, striking multiple cars (described as hitting four cars) and driving away. Herbert and Jo comment that the same incident involving a Tesla would receive massive global news coverage, while Waymo incidents receive relatively little scrutiny. They use this to illustrate the asymmetric media and regulatory treatment Tesla would face and why Tesla is being extremely cautious about deployment.

5. **Operational Infrastructure as the Remaining Bottleneck:** Beyond core AI, the hosts identify cloud connectivity, wireless charging, automated cleaning (robotic vacuums), AT&T connectivity reliability, and other meta-infrastructure as the true remaining barriers to robotaxi scaling. A specific example is cited where some Tesla robotaxis lost cloud connectivity and went dark mid-ride — the root cause was Tesla's cloud connection (possibly AWS), not AT&T. Jo argues these problems cannot be simulated and must be discovered and resolved through real-world deployment at scale.

## Market & Competition

1. **Why No Competitor Can Replicate Tesla's Infrastructure:** Jo Bhakdi argues that even if a competitor like Volkswagen, Toyota, or Mercedes were to match Tesla's FSD neural network capability today, they would still need years and billions of dollars to build out the surrounding operational infrastructure — cloud systems, connectivity layers, charging, cleaning, remote operations — that can only be stress-tested at real-world scale with massive fleets. He states no traditional automaker has even begun testing at scale, and that Nvidia's role is chip supplier, not vertically integrated robotaxi operator.

2. **Simulation Cannot Substitute for Real-World Scaling:** Jo Bhakdi directly rebuts the thesis that competitors could use Nvidia-powered simulation to accelerate their way to parity. He distinguishes between simulation of the neural net's perception/decision-making (which is simulatable) and the broader infrastructure reliability problems — cloud uptime, connectivity, edge-case operations — which are not simulatable and can only be discovered through deployment. He references a YouTube video by Dillon Loomis covering the connectivity issue as a concrete illustration.

3. **Tesla Vehicle Safety — Head-On Collision Survivability:** Herbert shares a Facebook post from a Tesla owner named Adrienne Rose Alvarado, who survived a head-on collision with a drunk driver, walked away with minor injuries (swelling, bruising, a fractured concern), while the drunk driver was ejected from his vehicle and hospitalized in the ICU. Jo Bhakdi explains the structural reason: Tesla EVs have no front engine, allowing the entire front section to function as a crumple zone without cabin intrusion, making them among the safest vehicles in head-on collisions.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**

- "Reports from the community are overwhelmingly positive saying this release is a magnitude leap from 14.3.1." — Herbert
- "It's a revamped, rearchitected model. I would not be surprised if we actually see significant improvements with every single iteration now." — Jo Bhakdi
- "Safety is solved. It's once you have safety, it's a tradeoff between convenience and safety." — Jo Bhakdi
- "The engineering problem is not just safety... to merge, to make it convenient and safe, that is a capability issue." — Jo Bhakdi
- "At the moment where this scales, at the moment you have tens of thousands of robotaxis in Dallas, Texas, Austin, whatever, it's game over." — Jo Bhakdi
- "You can't simulate your way out of it... This is a real-world safety-critical operation. You need to actually build it." — Jo Bhakdi
- Cybercab current production rate: ~10–12 per day; current fleet: ~640 deployed
- Waymo: ~3,000 cars, 5 cities, expanding to 10 cities in 2026
- Herbert's end-of-2026 fleet estimate: 15,000 Cybercabs produced; Jo Bhakdi's estimate: 10,000+ deployed in robotaxi service
- Jo Bhakdi's prior prediction: 1,800 robotaxis deployed by April/May 2026; actual: ~640–800
- Jo Bhakdi's calculation: 2,000 annualized robotaxi units ≈ ~5% of free cash flow; 15,000 units concentrated in December ≈ 1–2% of 2026 free cash flow

2026-04-28.title: Why Uber's Robotaxi Pivot Won't Save It
2026-04-28.body:
This video features Cern Basher interviewing a guest analyst who has written a two-part article series on Uber's strategic vulnerabilities in the face of autonomous vehicle deployment. The core thesis is that Uber's business model — which thrives on aggregating fragmented human driver supply — becomes structurally obsolete as the industry shifts toward a small number of companies owning large, consolidated autonomous fleets. The video systematically breaks down Uber's financials, its AV partnership strategy, and why the analyst believes Uber will ultimately be "shut out" of the robotaxi economy.

## Robotaxi
1. **Uber's AV Facilitator Ambition:** Uber has publicly stated it intends to be the largest facilitator of autonomous vehicle trips in the world by 2029, partnering with approximately 20 hardware platforms, self-driving technology providers, and fleet management companies. The analyst argues this strategy of partnering with "anybody that has a pulse" is a symptom of weakness, not strength — specifically driven by Tesla's refusal to partner with Uber.

2. **Tesla's Absence Is the Defining Gap:** The analyst emphasizes that Tesla is the one critical partner missing from Uber's AV roster and that Tesla has no interest in joining Uber's platform. Uber's CEO acknowledged this on stage, noting Tesla "doesn't play well with others" and takes a vertical approach. He expressed openness to Tesla joining if and when its camera-only FSD approach achieves a sufficient safety record, but acknowledged it remains "TBD." The analyst interprets Tesla's absence as a structural, not temporary, problem for Uber.

3. **Waymo Partnership Is Also Fragile:** Even Uber's existing partnership with Waymo is described as inherently unstable. The analyst argues that once Waymo reaches sufficient scale, it will have every economic incentive to cut out Uber entirely and capture the full revenue from rides rather than sharing it. The same logic applies to any AV provider — consolidated autonomous fleet operators will not want to share revenue with a middleman.

4. **Fragmented vs. Consolidated Supply — The Central Structural Shift:** The analyst's overarching framework is that Uber wins in a world of fragmented human supply (many individual drivers needing an aggregator) and loses in a world of consolidated autonomous supply (a few companies owning large fleets that self-direct demand). In the latter scenario, the "orchestra conductor" role Uber plays becomes unnecessary because the orchestra conducts itself. The analyst notes that if the AV industry ends up with 20 relatively equal players, Uber may retain relevance, but if it consolidates to 4–5 dominant players with significant market share, those players will simply deploy their own apps and bypass Uber entirely.

5. **Fleet Operator as Uber's Only Off-Ramp:** The analyst suggests the only viable survival path for Uber in an autonomous world is to abandon its current platform model and become a large fleet operator — essentially buying and owning autonomous vehicles at scale. He notes Uber already finances some Tesla purchases for drivers, but points out that actually owning a fleet would be an entirely different business model. He acknowledges other companies would pursue the same strategy, making that path competitive as well.

6. **AV Deployment Timeline — Uber's Conflicted Position:** An Uber document from February 4th is cited, in which Uber acknowledged that one year prior it expected AV commercialization to take much longer than the technology itself was advancing. The document outlined four prerequisites for wide AV deployment: a consistently superhuman safety record and enabling regulation; a cost-effective scaled hardware platform; excellent on-the-ground operations; and a high-utilization network managing variable demand. The analyst notes that only Tesla currently satisfies the "cost-effective scaled hardware platform" requirement, and that Uber actually benefits from slower AV commercialization timelines, which colors how they frame the challenges.

## Market & Competition
1. **Commoditization Argument — The Bull Case for Uber:** The video steelmans the Uber bull case: some investors argue that autonomous driving technology will be commoditized like other software, leading to many competing AV providers of roughly equal capability. In that scenario, an aggregator like Uber — analogous to Expedia in travel, a comparison Uber's CEO reportedly makes frequently — would remain essential. The analyst acknowledges this logic but argues it is unlikely to play out because AV development has extreme capital and data requirements that favor a winner-take-most outcome among a small number of players.

2. **Tens of Thousands of Teslas Already on Uber's Network:** Uber's CEO confirmed that tens of thousands of Teslas are already operating on the Uber platform, used by individual drivers — some of whom use FSD. The host clarifies this is not Uber owning Tesla vehicles; rather, individual drivers purchased or financed those cars themselves, and some financing was facilitated by Uber. This is described as meaningfully different from Uber operating an autonomous Tesla fleet.

## Financials
1. **Uber Q4 Financials — Revenue and Gross Bookings:** In Q4, Uber reported total revenue of $14.4 billion. Of that, $8.2 billion came from its core mobility (ride-hailing) segment with gross margins of approximately 27%, and approximately $5 billion came from Uber Eats with gross margins of approximately 21%. The freight segment contributed remaining revenue but was not yet profitable. Uber reported gross bookings of $54 billion in the quarter, meaning approximately $40 billion of customer payments flowed through to drivers — leaving only the $14.4 billion as Uber's recognized revenue.

2. **Uber's Thin Net Margins Despite Owning No Vehicles:** Despite operating as an asset-light platform that owns no vehicles, Uber's net profit was approximately $300 million on $14.4 billion in revenue, implying a net margin of roughly 2%. The analyst notes that operating profit on a normalized basis may be closer to a couple billion per quarter, suggesting a more sustainable operating margin of 10–12%, comparable to the low-margin automobile business. The host expresses surprise that an app-based business without physical assets doesn't earn 70–80% margins, and the analyst attributes this to the high cost of operating the platform's infrastructure and corporate overhead.

3. **Driver Cost Is the Core Value Destruction Mechanism:** The $40 billion paid to drivers out of $54 billion in gross bookings illustrates why autonomous vehicles are so economically disruptive — eliminating driver costs would theoretically allow whoever owns the AV fleet to retain the vast majority of gross bookings as revenue. But since Uber doesn't own the vehicles, it cannot capture that upside. The analyst frames this as the core reason Uber's platform model collapses in an autonomous world.

4. **Scale Economics and Path to Profitability:** The analyst notes that Uber only recently achieved profitability after more than 20 years of operation, describing it as a classic scale business where expanding into new markets requires absorbing losses before reaching unit economics that work. This structural dynamic, combined with Uber's thin current margins, makes the business particularly vulnerable to disruption at the exact moment it has finally become profitable.

Notable quotes and data:
- "The orchestra will conduct itself." — Guest analyst's metaphor for why Uber's aggregator role becomes unnecessary in an autonomous world.
- "Tesla doesn't play well with others." — Uber CEO's characterization of why Tesla is not on the platform.
- "When the day comes when those Teslas are safe with a camera-only approach, we'd love to have those Teslas on our platform." — Uber CEO, acknowledging Tesla's absence while leaving the door open.
- "By 2029, we think that we will facilitate more autonomous and robotaxi rides than anyone else in the world." — Uber's stated AV ambition.
- Uber Q4 gross bookings: $54 billion; recognized revenue: $14.4 billion; driver payments: ~$40 billion.
- Uber mobility gross margin: ~27%; Uber Eats gross margin: ~21%.
- Uber Q4 net profit: ~$300 million on $14.4 billion revenue (~2% net margin).
- Uber has ~20 AV partners across hardware, software, and fleet management.
- Uber document dated February 4th outlined four prerequisites for wide AV deployment.
- "Uber wins in a world of fragmented human supply. Uber loses in a world of consolidated autonomous supply." — Guest analyst's core thesis.

2026-04-28.title: Why Tesla Just Stopped the FSD Rollout & Elon's TSLA Sacrifice ⚡️
2026-04-28.body:
This video from the "electrified" channel covers a range of Tesla developments including the paused FSD 14.3.2 rollout, connectivity issues with the new Summon feature and robotaxi remote operations, Cybercab testing vehicle updates at Giga Texas, Elon Musk's 2018 compensation plan restructuring, and FSD regulatory progress in Europe. The host maintains a self-described objective stance, willing to call out Tesla's shortcomings alongside its progress. The video closes with a personal update from the creator about stepping away from a side business venture.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3.2 Rollout Paused:** The rollout of FSD version 14.3.2 has apparently been paused, according to noted FSD tester Chuck Cook. Cook's initial guess for the pause was related to the new "intervene" question screen — specifically, Tesla moved the interaction to multiple-choice only rather than voice-based, and initially omitted navigation as an option. Tesla engineer Yun Tasai acknowledged the navigation omission, responding "noted" when Luca suggested it should be added. The host, however, suspects the pause may be driven by deeper connectivity and infrastructure issues rather than just the UI change.

2. **Summon Now Unified with FSD Branch — But Plagued by Connectivity Issues:** The new "Actually Smart Summon" feature has been paired with robotaxi features in the FSD 14.3.2 branch, meaning all features now use a unified model. This has delivered notably improved parking lot behavior, though the feature is capped at 6 mph and has a radius the host considers too limited. However, Chuck Cook's testing revealed serious and repeated connectivity failures — the vehicle stopped mid-route, rolled past its destination after the button was released, and displayed errors including "summon not ready" and "waiting for improved phone location." Critically, both Cook's phone and the in-car Tesla UI showed full 5G signal bars throughout, suggesting the issue is not cellular signal strength.

3. **Cloud Infrastructure Likely the Root Cause:** The host explains that Summon operates through a four-step relay — from the user's phone network (e.g., Verizon), through the internet, through Tesla's cloud servers (historically hosted on Amazon Web Services), and then to AT&T before reaching the car. The host argues the connectivity failures are most likely a problem with Tesla's cloud relay infrastructure, not the cellular carriers, since both endpoints showed full bars. Because Summon is now paired with a much larger unified FSD model, latency and bandwidth demands have increased substantially, making cloud infrastructure performance a bigger challenge. The host views this as fixable on Tesla's own terms without requiring renegotiation with carriers.

4. **FSD Swerves onto Highway Shoulder — Impressive or Concerning?:** A user video of FSD 14.3.2 on the highway showed the vehicle making an evasive maneuver onto the shoulder at high speed over rumble strips, with seemingly nothing ahead. Shoke framed this as an example of FSD's 360-degree awareness, suggesting the car may have detected a threat behind it. The host acknowledged the potential upside — if FSD can detect fast-approaching rear traffic and make evasive maneuvers, that would be a meaningful safety capability — but noted the driver's calm non-reaction was striking.

5. **FSD Navigation Still Problematic, Though Improving:** The host noted that navigation issues persist in the 14.3.2 branch, sharing an image from user Dennis of a confusing navigation state. However, the host observed that most early access group videos suggest navigation has improved relative to the 14.2 branches, even if it remains far from acceptable for full deployment.

6. **Swedish FSD Approval — Employee Testing Only:** Supervised FSD has been approved for testing in Strängnäs, Sweden, but the host clarified this applies only to trained Tesla employees with a limited number of vehicles. This does not mean Tesla owners in Sweden can use supervised FSD. Finland, meanwhile, confirmed it will pursue EU approval through the TCMV process rather than a national fast-lane route, meaning it will wait for a broader European consensus.

7. **Chinese AI Engineers Validate Tesla's Autonomous Approach:** Two prominent Chinese AI engineers with their own autonomous driving startup publicly stated that Tesla's approach is the only viable path to Level 4 autonomy. They argued that Waymo's approach cannot fully solve the long-tail problem and that Waymo's city-by-city expansion costs are prohibitively high. One engineer, Yinshi, stated Tesla is still the global leader in intelligent driving and that other companies remain far behind. He also noted that China's AI large model parameter volume currently lags Tesla's due to compute infrastructure constraints, and that vehicle-side models industry-wide are too small, with tens of billions of parameters needed for comprehensive inference — a benchmark not yet met broadly.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Test Vehicles at Giga Texas — Steering Wheels Included:** Joe Tegtmeyer reported at least 15 more glossy deep-gold Cybercabs at Giga Texas, and these vehicles appear to be equipped with steering wheels and pedals. This is a meaningful distinction — earlier speculation was that glossy Cybercabs would be true production variants without any manual controls. The current expectation is these are test vehicles that will be shipped across the country for testing purposes. The host estimates that even 20 Cybercabs per state across 50 states would account for 1,000 vehicles, suggesting most of April and likely much of May will be occupied by test vehicle distribution rather than robotaxi network deployment.

2. **Robotaxi Network Still in Early Stages — Dallas and Houston at Two Vehicles Each:** The Dallas and Houston robotaxi deployments remain at only two unsupervised Model Y vehicles each, now on day 11 of operation. Austin has reached 15 unsupervised vehicles according to a third-party tracker. The host cautioned that the tracker's total figure of 640 includes inactive vehicles, and that its reported 23 unsupervised rides in Austin over the past week only reflects user-reported rides — actual ride volume is higher. The host also noted that Cybercabs could begin replacing Model Ys on the robotaxi network at any time, but Tesla may produce hundreds of Cybercabs before deploying even one to the network.

3. **Remote Operations Connectivity Also Problematic:** Separate from Summon's cloud relay issues, the robotaxi remote operations communications are also experiencing connectivity problems. Texas Tesla reported his mother's first robotaxi ride in Dallas was filled with glitches — the screen refused to work and rider support connections were poor and randomly dropped. User Spencer, described as a Tesla fan, said over half his rider support connections had "incredibly poor" connectivity, and that an average customer would not be happy with the experience. The host noted the mechanisms behind Summon and remote operations are different, but both are experiencing connection failures.

4. **Austin Robotaxi — Supervisors Back in Driver's Seat for Highway Rides:** Josh West reported from Austin that Tesla has returned supervisors to the driver's seat with hands on the wheel for rides that include highway segments. The host clarified Tesla is still adding new unsupervised vehicles in Austin and has not eliminated unsupervised rides, but highway-inclusive rides still use supervised drivers. West also reported a poor experience — after 15 minutes wait due to high demand, a Model Y with no robotaxi badging arrived and dropped the passengers approximately a quarter mile from their intended destination. The supervisor told them to call support, support said nothing could be done, and the passengers had to walk the remainder in 91°F heat.

5. **School Zone Speed Compliance Failure:** Texas Tesla shared a video showing the robotaxi failing to slow to 20 mph in an active school zone — the vehicle traveled at 35 mph during a period (3:05 PM on a school day) that fell within the posted 20 mph enforcement window (2:45–4:15 PM). The host flagged this as a meaningful safety compliance issue that needs to be addressed.

6. **Robotaxi App Now on Google Play Store:** The Tesla robotaxi app is now available for download on the Google Play Store for Android users.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi 3-Week Pilot with ISO Logistics:** A company called ISO Logistics has begun a 3-week pilot of the Tesla Semi on live freight routes, serving multiple customers. ISO stated it will release findings from the pilot after the evaluation period concludes. No performance or efficiency data was shared yet.

2. **Supercharger Network Gains Predictive Queue Intelligence:** Tesla has deployed a new model for its Supercharger network that uses real-time traffic monitoring and vehicle trajectory data within a geofence around Supercharger sites to predict occupancy and queue length. The model reduces queue length estimation error to 20%, meaning in cases of 10 or more vehicles waiting, the predicted queue is accurate within one to two vehicles. The system is now deployed globally. Tesla also released a digital queue feature via the app, allowing drivers to join a virtual line rather than physically waiting at the station. The host noted that challenges remain, including cars queuing at nearby drive-throughs affecting estimates, as seen at the Tesla Diner.

## Market & Competition

1. **Waymo Scalability Questioned by Chinese Engineers:** The two Chinese autonomous driving engineers cited above argued specifically that Waymo's HD map-dependent, city-by-city approach cannot solve the long-tail problem and that the cost of expanding to new cities is prohibitively large. They positioned Tesla's vision-based, generalized approach as the only scalable path to Level 4, and noted Tesla is already ahead on addressing compute and memory constraints that will challenge the broader industry over the next 2–3 years.

## Financials

1. **Elon's 2018 Compensation Plan Restructured — Lock-Up Through 2033:** Tesla's special committee reached a new agreement governing how Elon Musk can exercise his 2018 performance award of approximately 303–304 million shares. Under the new implementation agreement, Elon can exercise the shares between May 21st and August 15th, 2026. Upon exercise, the shares will be issued as restricted stock rather than freely tradable. Elon must remain in continuous service as CEO or a specific executive role through January 19th, 2028 for the shares to vest and become non-forfeitable. A 5-year holding period begins at the vesting date (not the exercise date), meaning Elon could not begin selling until approximately January 2033. Voting rights are granted immediately upon exercise. The host characterized this as Elon making meaningful concessions — delaying his own liquidity for the benefit of Tesla and reducing potential market disruption from large share sales.

2. **SEC Filing Clarifications — No New Dilution, No Selling:** The host clarified two recent SEC filings that caused confusion. The S-8 filing was Tesla legally registering the 303 million shares so they can be issued to Elon once he exercises his options — not new dilution and not a sale. The Form 4 showing Elon "disposing" of 96 million shares was him relinquishing access to a bridge loan that Tesla had set up as a contingency in case his 2018 compensation plan was permanently rejected by the courts — since the plan was restored, the bridge loan is no longer needed.

3. **TSLA Stock Price:** Tesla stock closed the day at $378.67, up 6.3%, while the Nasdaq was up 0.1%. Volume was in line with the average.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**
- Yinshi (Chinese AI engineer): *"I believe Tesla is still the global leader in intelligent driving, and other companies are still far behind."*
- Yinshi: *"Tens of billions of parameters are the benchmark for comprehensive inference capabilities and current vehicle side models are too small leaving significant room for improvement in the next 2 to 3 years."*
- Spencer (Tesla fan, on rider support): *"Over half the times I've connected to Rider support, the connectivity has been incredibly poor. If I was an average customer, I would not be very happy."*
- Supercharger queue model: reduces queue length estimation error to 20%; in 10+ vehicle wait scenarios, predicts queue within 1–2 vehicles
- At least 15 glossy Cybercabs now spotted at Giga Texas, all equipped with steering wheels and pedals
- Austin robotaxi: 15 unsupervised vehicles per third-party tracker; only 23 rides reported in past 7 days (user-reported only)
- Dallas and Houston: 2 unsupervised Model Y vehicles each, day 11 of operation
- Tesla stock: $378.67, +6.3% on the day vs. Nasdaq +0.1%
- Elon's exercise window: May 21 – August 15, 2026; vesting date: January 19, 2028; share sale lock-up until approximately January 2033

2026-04-28.title: Tesla Stock Outlook And Key Catalysts
2026-04-28.body:
This video is a casual, conversational discussion between host Brian (Futurazza) and guest Randy Kirk covering recent Tesla stock news, short-term price movements, and financial performance. The core thesis is that recent negative stock reactions — particularly around Elon Musk's 2018 pay award share registration — were overblown and algorithmically driven, and that Tesla's financial fundamentals are improving. The tone is informal and editorial, with limited hard data but notable commentary on per-vehicle profitability and tax-related FUD.

## Financials
1. **Elon Musk's 2018 Pay Award Share Registration:** Tesla officially registered approximately 304 million shares related to Elon Musk's 2018 compensation award, making them freely tradable. The stock dropped sharply on the news, which the hosts attributed to algorithmic trading reacting to headlines without understanding the context. The hosts emphasized this was not new information — it had been known for years — and that the market reaction was a knee-jerk overreaction. Randy noted that some of the shares are subject to a five-year lockup period, meaning not all of them could be exercised in 2028 as some reports implied.

2. **Tax Coverage Mechanism:** Randy explained that the tax obligation on Elon's stock award is likely to be handled through a "net settlement" or "cover" mechanism, where Tesla itself pays the taxes by withholding a portion of the shares rather than Elon selling shares on the open market. This would mean the actual number of shares entering circulation would be lower than the headline figure. The strike price on the options was noted as $23 per share, meaning they are deeply in the money.

3. **Per-Vehicle Profitability Recovery:** The video references a Motley Fool article noting that Tesla's net profit per vehicle, which once exceeded $10,000 per car in 2022–2023, fell to less than half that by 2024, but has since recovered to approximately $5,558 per vehicle. Randy contextualized the earlier peak as an artifact of COVID-era supply shortages and price increases Elon deliberately implemented to prevent middlemen from profiting on resales — not a reflection of structural improvement in Tesla's cost structure. He suggested a "normal" per-vehicle profit is around $6,000, and that the current recovery toward that level is healthy and expected.

4. **Tesla's Tax Payments:** In response to a viral claim that individual taxpayers pay more in taxes than Tesla, Brian stated that Tesla paid over $1 billion in taxes last year. He and Randy discussed how Tesla's lower U.S. tax burden reflects legitimate tax code provisions — including recognition of prior losses and R&D investment credits — rather than evasion.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Delivery and Revenue Softness vs. Margin Improvement:** The hosts referenced the Motley Fool article's framing that Tesla's Q1 2026 results were "not as bad as the post-earnings stock drop suggested." Quarterly deliveries were described as lackluster, leading to disappointing revenue, but gross margins were noted as "pretty fantastic." The implication is that Tesla is prioritizing profitability over volume in the near term.

2. **Supercharger Queue System:** Tesla has introduced a virtual queue system for Supercharger stations, operating on an honor system to manage congestion. Brian noted this is particularly relevant in high-demand areas like Colorado cities and Santa Monica (described as "probably the busiest charger in the world," which now has a second location). The hosts viewed this as a practical but modest improvement, with Tesla's data capabilities well-positioned to guide future Supercharger network expansion.

## Market & Competition
1. **Stock Volatility and Algorithmic Trading:** The hosts observed that Tesla's stock dropped aggressively in morning trading on the day of recording (Monday, April 28, 2026) before recovering into positive territory. Brian attributed the dip to trading algorithms that flagged the share registration news without being able to parse the nuance — specifically, that the shares are deeply in-the-money options with tax coverage mechanisms and lockup restrictions, not a straightforward dilution event.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla registered approximately **304 million shares** related to Elon Musk's 2018 pay award
- Options strike price: **$23 per share**
- Options begin expiring in **2028**, with some subject to a **five-year lockup**
- Tesla paid over **$1 billion in taxes** last year
- Net profit per vehicle peaked at **over $10,000** in 2022–2023, fell to **less than half** (~$4,000–$5,000) by 2024, and has recovered to approximately **$5,558**
- Randy's estimate of "normal" per-vehicle profit: approximately **$6,000**
- Brian predicted the stock would reach **$410** that day — acknowledged as a miss
- Randy's upcoming events: **June 6** Tesla meetup in Muskegon; **July 2–4** Long View Go Forth Festival in Klickitat County, Washington

2026-04-28.title: The Gas Truck Industry Didn’t See This Coming | OEVA 2026
2026-04-28.body:
This video is a presentation by Brian from the YouTube channel "futureaza," delivered at what appears to be the OEVA (Oregon Electric Vehicle Association) 2026 event. The talk covers the current state of electric semi-trucks, their advantages over diesel, who manufactures them, the cost landscape, and the key obstacles slowing broader adoption.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Environmental and Health Advantages of Electric Semis:** Brian outlines that electric big rigs are 80–90% cleaner than diesel when charged from the grid, even accounting for fossil fuel usage in electricity generation. Studies from 2019-era grids (which were 63% fossil fuel) showed 50–65% emissions reductions. Beyond emissions, electric trucks are perceptibly about half as loud as diesel trucks in normal operation, and regenerative braking dramatically reduces brake dust — which contains metals like copper, iron, barium, and antimony and forms PM2.5 particles capable of entering the bloodstream through the lungs.

2. **Operating Cost Savings:** A diesel semi consumes fuel at 50–70 cents per mile, while an electric semi costs 15–25 cents per mile — a savings of $15,000–$25,000 per year of operation. Electric trucks also require significantly less maintenance: no oil changes, minimal brake wear, and no motor rebuilds at high mileage. Brian suggests that at a $250,000 purchase price with these savings, the truck could effectively pay for itself over 10 years.

3. **The Tesla Semi:** Brian highlights the Tesla Semi as an exceptional product, offering 500 miles of range fully loaded, the lowest operating cost among US manufacturers, and a gross vehicle weight allowance of 82,000 lbs (versus the standard 80,000 lbs cap for diesel), meaning cargo capacity is on par with diesel. The Tesla Semi weighs only about 2,000 lbs more than a comparable diesel truck. The factory in Sparks, Nevada is nearly complete — Brian visited a couple of months prior and confirmed the building and outfitting are mostly done — with production expected to begin in 2026. Hundreds of units have already been sold to clients like Pepsi and Frito-Lay for fleet testing. Tesla Semi pricing from California incentive invoices has been observed in the $240,000–$260,000 range, though Brian notes Tesla may be losing money at that price.

4. **Battery Technology in the Tesla Semi:** The current Tesla Semi uses Panasonic 2170 cells manufactured in Reno, Nevada. Tesla plans to transition to 4680 cells produced in Texas. Brian notes that EVs overall are approximately 20 times less likely to catch fire than a gasoline vehicle, and hybrids are 20 times more likely to burn than a pure EV. Most Chinese electric semis use LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries, which are very difficult to ignite and have strong longevity.

5. **Regenerative Braking on the Tesla Semi:** Brian describes the Tesla Semi's primary route as Sparks, Nevada to Fremont, California, traversing Donner Pass daily. The regenerative braking system means the truck can recover energy on the descent — arriving at the bottom of the mountain with more charge than at the top — and brakes may barely be touched while fully loaded. Brian notes that the Tesla Semi has never jacknifed, attributing this partly to computer-assisted traction control systems that are common across newer Class 8 trucks.

## Market & Competition

1. **Manufacturer Landscape:** Brian surveys the US and global market for electric Class 8 semis. US manufacturers include Freightliner (eCascadia, made in Portland), Kenworth (made in Renton, Washington), Mack (primarily garbage trucks, made in Pennsylvania), BYD (made in China, assembled in Los Angeles), and International (San Antonio). European options include Volvo, Mercedes (sharing R&D with the eCascadia under the Daimler group), and Scania. China is described as going very aggressive on electric freight, with projections of 100% electric trucking by 2030–2035, driven by energy security concerns given China's limited domestic oil supply.

2. **Pricing Tiers:** Diesel semis cost $150,000–$180,000. Legacy OEM electric trucks (eCascadia, Volvo) come in at $400,000–$500,000, even for large orders. Purpose-built EV semi companies — BYD, Windrose, and Tesla — are pricing in the $180,000–$280,000 range. Brian identifies $300,000 as the critical price threshold: below that, 10-year operating savings of $150,000–$250,000 make the purchase economically viable. In China, comparable electric semis cost $60,000–$180,000.

3. **Two Manufacturing Approaches and Their Trade-offs:** Brian contrasts two approaches to building electric semis. The "purpose-built" approach (Tesla, BYD, Windrose) requires approximately $2 billion upfront to build a new factory and design the truck from scratch, but produces a more cost-competitive and longer-range product. The "converted platform" approach (Freightliner, Volvo, etc.) saves roughly $1 billion upfront by electrifying existing platforms, but results in each truck costing approximately $150,000 more than it should and delivering less range than a purpose-built EV.

4. **Policy Headwinds:** Brian identifies several US policy changes acting as obstacles to EV truck adoption: the EPA's repeal of greenhouse gas endangerment findings, elimination of the qualified commercial clean vehicle tax credit, restrictions on EV charging infrastructure funding, increased tariffs on Chinese EV components, and federal legal actions preempting state-level Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandates.

5. **Charging Infrastructure:** Freightliner currently has the largest charging network for electric semis in the US, with dozens of locations. Tesla is building out its semi-charging network more slowly due to lower current demand. Most trucks are converging on the Megawatt Charging Standard (MCS), which supports up to 1 megawatt of charging. The eCascadia currently uses CCS1 (dual-handle), a legacy of being developed before MCS existed. Brian notes that adequate and affordable charging infrastructure is critical to the economics of electric trucking.

Notable quotes and data:
- Diesel semi fuel cost: 50–70 cents per mile; electric semi: 15–25 cents per mile
- Annual operating savings: $15,000–$25,000 per year
- Tesla Semi range: 500 miles fully loaded
- Tesla Semi GVWR: 82,000 lbs (vs. 80,000 lbs for diesel)
- Tesla Semi price (from California rebate invoices): $240,000–$260,000
- Legacy OEM electric semi prices: $400,000–$500,000
- Purpose-built EV semi prices: $180,000–$280,000
- Diesel semi prices: $150,000–$180,000
- Chinese electric semi prices: $60,000–$180,000
- Cost to build a purpose-built EV semi factory: ~$2 billion
- EVs are approximately 20 times less likely to catch fire than gasoline vehicles
- China projected to reach 100% electric trucking by 2030–2035
- Tesla Semi battery: currently Panasonic 2170 cells (Reno, NV); transitioning to 4680 cells (Texas)
- Tesla Semi's primary operational route: Sparks, NV to Fremont, CA over Donner Pass
- "The real sweet spot is 300,000. If you can get it under 300,000 to your door, it can make sense."

2026-04-28.title: Why Tesla Stock Is Ready To Make a BIG MOVE
2026-04-28.body:
This video is a portfolio performance update from Jo Bhakdi of The Tesla Thesis, covering the Pioneer Reserve and Pioneer Alpha investment vehicles. The core thesis is that Tesla is fundamentally stronger now than it was at its all-time highs in December 2025, yet trades at a significant discount, making a return to $400 likely in the near term. The video also touches briefly on the robotaxi and Optimus narratives as longer-term catalysts, while the bulk of the content focuses on trading strategy, portfolio performance, and a new bond product launch.

## Financials

1. **Pioneer Alpha outperforms Tesla by 21% year-to-date:** As of Monday, April 27, 2026, the Pioneer Alpha portfolio is up 5.23% year-to-date while Tesla is down significantly, producing a 21% alpha over Tesla for the year. In a single week (April 20–27), Pioneer Alpha was up 1.59% while Tesla was down 3.52%, generating a weekly alpha of 5.11%. Jo Bhakdi attributes this to correctly anticipating the earnings call — predicting that the drop ahead of earnings was overdone and that the results would not carry major negative surprises, positioning the portfolio with out-of-the-money short puts accordingly.

2. **Long-term portfolio alpha is substantial:** Since inception on January 1, 2024 (approximately two years of systematic trading), Pioneer Alpha has generated 54% alpha over Tesla. Over the past six months, the portfolio leads the S&P 500 by 3.55%, and year-to-date it leads the S&P by approximately 43% on a relative basis. The portfolio holds concentrated positions in AI-related equities including Tesla, Nvidia, MicroStrategy, and Robinhood, supplemented by tactical options strategies.

3. **New Pioneer Alpha bond launched:** Jo Bhakdi announces a new three-year bond issued through the Pioneer Reserve Luxembourg securitization vehicle, linked directly to the Pioneer Alpha portfolio. The bond carries a 1.5% annual operating expense, a three-year maturity, and pays bond holders Tesla's return as a baseline plus 50% of any additional alpha Pioneer Alpha generates above Tesla. On the downside, bond holders absorb half the loss if Pioneer Alpha underperforms Tesla. The product is restricted to accredited investors in the United States and qualified investors in Europe.

4. **Current options positioning targets $400 Tesla:** Jo Bhakdi states he is heavily positioned in short puts with a break-even point of approximately $372 by end of the week of April 28, 2026. He states that above $385, the position becomes highly profitable, and his primary thesis is that Tesla returns to $400 in the near term. He describes this as a probabilistic bet contingent on no major macro deterioration.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla trading at a large discount to December all-time highs:** Tesla reached an all-time high of $490 on December 16, 2025. As of the video date, Tesla is approximately $115–$120 below that level, while reference indices like the NASDAQ and S&P 500 are near or at all-time highs. Jo Bhakdi argues this disconnect is irrational given that Tesla as a company is fundamentally stronger today than it was in December.

2. **Tesla showing relative strength versus NASDAQ on a down day:** On the day of recording, the NASDAQ was down 1.37% while Tesla was only down 1.14%, which Jo Bhakdi interprets as bullish given Tesla's historical beta of approximately two (implying it would normally fall roughly twice the NASDAQ's move). He cites this relative outperformance as supporting evidence for his $400 near-term target.

3. **Nvidia dragged down by OpenAI news:** Nvidia, the portfolio's second-largest position, fell approximately 3.7% on the day of recording due to reports that OpenAI cannot purchase enough chips — news Jo Bhakdi characterizes as "fake" and inconsequential given what he describes as essentially unlimited demand for compute. He views the selloff as a buying opportunity.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab production versus autonomous capability gap:** Jo Bhakdi notes the apparent contradiction at the center of the current Tesla debate — Cybercabs are being produced in volume and are vehicles that can only effectively operate without a driver, yet Tesla has not yet demonstrated the ability to run them unsupervised at scale. He describes this as a pivotal and unresolved tension for investors, referencing broader debate over whether the earnings call signaled a slowdown in robotaxi deployment timelines.

2. **Scaling threshold for stock repricing:** Jo Bhakdi reiterates his existing thesis that reaching approximately 1,800 unsupervised robotaxis in operation represents a key inflection point — what he calls a "forcing function." He believes that scaling into the thousands or tens of thousands of robotaxis would trigger a stock repricing that could take Tesla to $1,000. He emphasizes, however, that Tesla does not need to reach this threshold to return to all-time highs.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus announcement referenced as near-term catalyst:** Jo Bhakdi briefly references a prior video in which he discussed an Optimus announcement expected within 90 days from the time of that video. No additional specifics are provided in this update, but it is cited alongside robotaxi as a key part of the ongoing Tesla investment narrative being tracked by the platform.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla all-time high: **$490 on December 16, 2025**
- Current Tesla discount to all-time high: approximately **$115–$120**
- Pioneer Alpha weekly alpha over Tesla (April 20–27, 2026): **+5.11%**
- Pioneer Alpha year-to-date return: **+5.23%**; Tesla year-to-date alpha: **+21%**
- Pioneer Alpha alpha since inception (Jan 1, 2024): **+54% over Tesla**
- Six-month alpha over S&P 500: **+3.55%**
- Jo Bhakdi's short put break-even: **$372**; highly profitable above **$385**; primary target: **$400**
- Nvidia down **3.7%** on the day due to OpenAI-related chip demand headlines
- NASDAQ down **1.37%** vs. Tesla down **1.14%** on the recording day
- New Pioneer Alpha bond: **3-year maturity**, **1.5% annual operating expenses**, returns Tesla benchmark + **50% of excess alpha**
- Robotaxi scaling threshold cited: **1,800 unsupervised robotaxis** as the key inflection point
- Potential stock target if robotaxi scales: **$1,000**
- *"We are dealing with a massive discount on the company right now."*
- *"All-time highs for Tesla do not require anything specific. It does not require robo taxi to scale to tremendous heights."*

2026-04-28.title: BYD Shark Hybrid System Explained
2026-04-28.body:
This video from Munro Live, hosted by Paul Turnbull, revisits the BYD Shark pickup truck's hybrid powertrain system to explain the engineering rationale behind extended range electric vehicles (EREVs) for truck applications. The core thesis is that for use cases like pickup trucks — which must handle both daily commuting and heavy towing — an EREV architecture can outperform a pure battery electric approach by trading a large battery pack for a smaller one supplemented by an internal combustion engine and a sophisticated clutch-based hybrid system. The video uses actual hardware components from a BYD Shark teardown to walk through how the system works mechanically.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **BYD Shark EREV Architecture and Battery Cost Trade-off:** Rather than equipping the Shark with a large ~130 kWh battery pack as a pure EV would require, BYD opted for a 30 kWh battery and used the approximately $10,000 in savings to add a turbocharged four-cylinder internal combustion engine and a hybrid drivetrain system. This allows the vehicle to function as a fully electric vehicle for daily commutes of up to 60 miles, while also being capable of operating as a conventional gasoline-powered truck for longer trips or heavy towing duties.

2. **Series vs. Parallel Hybrid Operation:** The BYD Shark primarily operates as a series hybrid — the internal combustion engine drives a generator, which charges the battery, which then powers front and rear electric motors. This keeps the engine running at its optimal efficiency point. However, because the electrical energy conversion chain (engine → generator → battery → motor) involves multiple efficiency losses (approximately 95% per electrical conversion step), this approach is less efficient than a direct mechanical connection. To address this, the system includes a clutch that can lock the internal combustion engine directly to the front wheels during highway cruising, effectively making it a parallel hybrid with near-99% mechanical efficiency for that power path.

3. **Clutch Mechanism Enabling Mode Switching:** The clutch at the heart of the system uses interlocking metal and carbon friction plates, hydraulically actuated, to allow variable degrees of engagement. When the clutch is open, the electric motor drives the front wheels independently. When the clutch is closed, the internal combustion engine drives the front wheels directly through a differential. The rear wheels are powered separately via the electric motor, allowing all-wheel drive when needed — such as when towing up a steep grade — by running the generator from the engine to supply power to the rear motor.

4. **Practical Towing and Refueling Advantages:** For towing applications such as pulling a trailer up a long hill, the system can simultaneously run the internal combustion engine to drive the front wheels directly while also generating electricity to power the rear motor, delivering strong combined output. For long-distance towing, the gasoline tank can be refilled at any conventional gas station in approximately five minutes, eliminating the range anxiety and charging time constraints associated with pure battery electric trucks.

## Market & Competition
1. **Industry Trend Toward EREV for Trucks:** Paul Turnbull notes that multiple automakers are now shifting from pure battery electric to extended range electric vehicle architectures, and highlights the BYD Shark as a leading example of this trend, particularly relevant for pickup truck applications where versatility between daily commuting and heavy-duty use is essential.

2. **Three Hybrid Architectures Compared:** Munro Live categorizes hybrids into three types: series hybrids (engine drives a generator, motors drive the wheels), parallel hybrids (engine and motor can both drive the wheels directly, as seen in vehicles like the Toyota Land Cruiser), and power-split hybrids (as seen in the Toyota Prius, described as currently the dominant hybrid form across applications). The BYD Shark is characterized as primarily a series hybrid with parallel capability when the clutch is engaged.

Notable quotes and data:
- BYD Shark battery size: **30 kWh** (vs. an implied ~130 kWh for a comparable pure EV)
- Cost savings from smaller battery: approximately **$10,000**, redirected to the ICE and hybrid system
- Pure electric range: **60 miles** for daily commuting
- Electrical conversion efficiency per step: approximately **95%** (generator and motor stages)
- Direct mechanical (clutch-locked) drivetrain efficiency: approximately **99%**
- Hardware provided for teardown by partner **A2AC1**
- Host: **Paul Turnbull**, Munro Live

2026-04-28.title: Daily X Summary (2026-04-28)
2026-04-28.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts are headlined by two meaningful autonomous driving signals: Tesla receiving approval to test FSD (Supervised) on public roads in Sweden, and firsthand reporting on a notably improved Actually Smart Summon experience — both pointing to continued FSD geographic expansion and capability maturation. Secondary themes include growing Cybercab sighting normalization, Tesla Semi commercial pilots, and the Model S/X discontinuation narrative. The overall signal is modestly bullish, with regulatory progress in Europe and real-world FSD performance standing out as the day's highest-value items.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD Approved for Public Road Testing in Sweden:** Tesla has received approval from Sweden's Transport Agency (Transportstyrelsen) to test FSD (Supervised) on public municipal roads in Strängnäs, Sweden. The approval is valid for one year following final agency sign-off, requires safety drivers, and covers municipal roads — noting that Tesla already holds state road approvals in Sweden. This is a meaningful regulatory milestone for Tesla's European FSD expansion, demonstrating that the supervised autonomy framework is gaining traction outside the U.S. market. The post drew strong engagement (2.4K likes, 259 reposts), signaling significant investor and enthusiast interest.

2. **Actually Smart Summon Impresses in Real-World Testing:** Sawyer Merritt reported spending approximately one hour riding in the back seat of his Model Y using the updated Actually Smart Summon across four different parking lots, including busy ones. He noted the car handled all scenarios "very well," with behavior so natural that bystanders barely noticed. This firsthand account suggests meaningful improvement in low-speed autonomous maneuvering — a capability directly relevant to robotaxi readiness — though no specific software version was cited.

3. **FSD UI Update — Navigation Added as Disengagement Reason:** A code or UI discovery reveals that "navigation" will be added as a selectable disengagement reason in an upcoming FSD popup. This is a minor but notable signal suggesting Tesla is refining its data collection granularity around why drivers intervene, which could improve training pipelines and safety reporting transparency.

4. **Cybercab Sightings Normalizing:** Merritt commented positively on the increasing frequency of Cybercab sightings becoming "a normal thing," accompanied by media. While no specific production or deployment numbers were provided, the tone reflects growing confidence that Cybercab pre-production or testing activity is visibly accelerating.

5. **Model S/X Discontinuation Framing — Software-Defined Vehicle Legacy:** Auto journalist Jason Cammisa offered commentary (quoted by Merritt across multiple posts) on Tesla's decision to discontinue the Model S/X, attributing it partly to the prohibitive cost of reengineering the platform to meet evolving safety regulations and the declining luxury segment. Cammisa also praised Tesla's software-defined vehicle approach, noting a nearly 10-year-old Model S still drove itself autonomously — contrasting it with legacy EVs like the VW e-Golf that shipped static and never updated. These posts reinforce Tesla's software moat narrative but carry no new financial data.

6. **Tesla Semi Commercial Pilot Underway:** AiLO Logistics, a freight brokerage and asset-based carrier, has begun a three-week pilot of the Tesla Semi on live freight routes serving multiple customers. No mileage, range, or financial terms were disclosed. This is a incremental commercial validation data point for the Semi program.

7. **Elon Musk 2018 Compensation Package — SEC Filing:** Tesla filed an S-8 statement with the SEC to register 303,960,630 shares of common stock for Elon Musk under his 2018 performance-based compensation package, following the Delaware Supreme Court's restoration of the award in December 2025. Merritt characterized this as expected and procedural. Investors should note the dilution figure (approximately 304 million shares) as a known but now formally registered event.

8. **Starlink Aviation Milestones (Tangential):** Starlink announced 2Gbps+ capable installations on commercial aircraft, and Emirates confirmed Starlink installation on its A380 fleet (three antennas per aircraft). These are SpaceX/Starlink developments with no direct Tesla operating impact, included for completeness given Musk ecosystem relevance.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — FSD regulatory expansion into Europe and improved real-world Summon performance are genuine incremental positives for the autonomy thesis, though no major catalyst or hard production/deployment number emerged today.

2026-04-29.title: Executive Summary (2026-04-29)
2026-04-29.body:
## Unsupervised Robotaxi Fleet

| City    |  Now |  1D |  7D |  30D |
|:--------|-----:|----:|----:|-----:|
| Austin  |   19 |  +4 |  +6 |  +10 |
| Dallas  |    3 |  +1 |  +1 |   +3 |
| Houston |    3 |  +1 |  +1 |   +3 |
| **Total** | **25** | +6 | +8 | +16 |

Source: [RobotaxiTracker.com](https://robotaxitracker.com/)

---

## Brief

- FSD V14.3.2 rolling out broadly to Tesla fleet, new disengagement category added.
- Tesla Semi first unit off high-volume Nevada production line.
- HW3 owners in 29 countries file €6.5M collective FSD claim.
- Cybercab Autonomy Pop-Up launches Miami F1 Grand Prix Fan Fest.
- Active Robotaxi fleet: 649 per RobotaxiTracker.com.
- Analyst price targets: $465–$550 range; capex raised $5B to $25B total.

## Autonomous Driving
- **FSD V14.3.2 broad rollout underway.** Software version 2026.2.9.9 is being pushed to a significantly larger owner group, with a new "Navigation" disengagement reason added to the FSD popup — a refinement to Tesla's disengagement taxonomy that may support future unsupervised deployment requirements.
- **Tesla Safety Score V3.0 launches in Florida and Maryland.** New policyholders gain access immediately; existing policyholders transition July 12th. The primary new feature is night driving as a scored behavior category, adding nighttime behavioral data to Tesla's insurance and FSD training flywheel.
- **Tesla promises FSD V14 Lite for international HW3 owners — with no timeline.** Tesla posted on X that V14 Lite will expand internationally after the U.S. HW3 rollout completes, subject to technical verification, regional adaptation, and regulatory approvals. The U.S. HW3 rollout is targeted for end of June 2026, meaning international owners are waiting well into H2 2026 at the earliest.
- **HW3 collective claim crystallizes: ~3,000 owners, 29 countries, €6.5M.** Tesla's first European FSD approval (Netherlands) was restricted to HW4, prompting a Dutch Model 3 owner to launch a collective claim site. Tesla confirmed at Q1 2026 earnings that HW3 "simply does not have the capability to achieve unsupervised FSD." Tesla separately announced plans for dedicated micro-factories to retrofit approximately 4 million HW3 vehicles worldwide; HW4 Plus (doubled memory) was announced one day after the earnings call, raising questions about the upgrade cycle.
- **AI5 chip tape-out cited as key structural catalyst by Cantor Fitzgerald.** The milestone was referenced as a central pillar of the bull thesis and was a reason multiple institutional analysts held their ratings through the post-earnings retail selloff.
- **Genma's technical moat thesis: quantization-aware training on AI4 chips during every training epoch.** Anonymous 15-year ADAS engineer "Genma_JP" argues Tesla's most underappreciated moat is its Cortex cluster — ~40,000 AI4 in-car chips mixed with ~90,000 H100 GPUs — which runs inference on actual vehicle silicon during training, making the deployed model bit-exact with the trained model. He quotes Elon at the 2025 shareholders meeting: *"You actually have to train for integer inference — which everyone else is training for floating point."* Q1 2026 earnings referenced 150,000 H100-equivalent GPUs in Tesla's training infrastructure.
- **FSD Supervised earns positive first impressions in South Korea.** A South Korean reporter described the system as flawlessly handling traffic signal compliance, lane keeping, speed limits, merging, and direction changes — meaningful qualitative signal for international FSD expansion.

## Robotaxi
- **Active Robotaxi fleet: 649 (all modes); unsupervised fleet: 25.** Per RobotaxiTracker.com as of April 30, 2026. Breakdown: Bay Area 542, Austin 101, Dallas 3, Houston 3 (active total); Austin 19, Dallas 3, Houston 3 (unsupervised subset).
- **Bhakdi acknowledges fleet miss but maintains 10,000–20,000 Cybercabs by year-end.** Bhakdi's pre-earnings prediction of ~1,800 unsupervised robotaxis by April/May 2026 was not met; he self-assesses the miss at 2–3 months and projects ~800–900 vehicles by end of May at a ~50–100%/month growth rate. His year-end target of 10,000–20,000 deployed Cybercabs is unchanged. The host's personal estimate is ~15,000.
- **Cybercab hardware in active logistics movement.** Two separate semi trucks loaded with Cybercabs were spotted on April 28th — the second such sighting in a single day — consistent with pre-launch fleet staging activity.
- **Tesla Autonomy Pop-Up opens in Miami at F1 Grand Prix Fan Fest.** Starting April 29th at Lummus Park, attendees can see the Cybercab in person and meet Optimus during the Crypto.com Miami Grand Prix Fan Fest — placing both products in front of a large, affluent, high-visibility international audience.
- **Cybercab production rate referenced at ~300/month currently.** Per Bhakdi, observing increments of 10–20 units at a time. He reasons that if the rate doubles monthly, the fleet exceeds 10,000 by year-end. The host flags Cybercab production above 5,000 units at the Q2 2026 earnings (expected late July) as the manufacturing moat validation threshold.
- **Current operational issues are connectivity-related, not FSD-related.** Bhakdi, citing Dillon Loomis, identifies that known Cybercab service disruptions — screen blackouts, vehicles stopping — stem from AWS/server connection drops, not from FSD failures. Elon described remaining friction on the Q1 call as "convenience issues": frozen red lights, construction zone loops, pickup/dropoff logistics.
- **Cybercab structural cost advantage over Waymo quantified.** Per analysis presented by Brian (Futurazza): Cybercab ~$25,000–$30,000 to produce, ~4,000 parts, no paint shop needed, 500,000–1,000,000-mile target lifespan. Waymo's Jaguar iPace estimated at ~$150,000 per vehicle; Zoox at ~$250,000. Waymo prices ~$4/mile and is not yet profitable; Tesla is pricing Austin rides at ~$1.50/mile with a projected target of ~$1/mile and ~$0.50 profit per mile.
- **Waymo's HD map approach described as a structural scaling ceiling.** Genma argues every construction zone, repaved road, or power outage renders the map wrong, requiring constant human maintenance. Real failure cases cited include Waymo vehicles frozen in Nashville intersections requiring police intervention, and vehicles blocked in Phoenix and Houston construction zones. His conclusion: "The HD map is not a feature. It is proof that the intelligence is missing." Waymo's Zeekr next-gen platform is separately undermined by the 100% U.S. tariff on Chinese-made vehicles.

## Humanoid Bots
- **Optimus summer 2026 production ramp on track.** Per Farzad-FM, Tesla's Fremont factory is described as pivoting toward humanoid robot production, with a long-term target of millions of units per year. The ramp is cited as a core reason Elon seeks to step back from day-to-day CEO duties.

## Electric Vehicles
- **First Tesla Semi rolls off high-volume production line at Giga Nevada.** The dedicated 1.7-million-square-foot factory adjacent to Gigafactory Nevada is designed for 50,000 trucks/year, with analysts projecting 5,000–15,000 deliveries in 2026 (Electrek's author considers the high end optimistic). Two trims: Standard Range ~$260,000 (325 miles), Long Range $290,000 (500 miles) — both positioned as lowest-priced Class 8 BEV tractors on the market. In California's Clean Truck voucher program (Jan 2025–Feb 2026), Tesla Semi accounted for 965 of 1,067 applications.
- **MDB Transportation launches 3-week Tesla Semi pilot at Ports of LA and Long Beach.** The Compton-based drayage operator is tracking energy efficiency, cycle time, and driver experience — the second port trucking company to deploy the Semi commercially. Hight Logistics (Long Beach) also took delivery earlier in 2026 and plans fleet expansion.
- **Megacharger network: 66 locations mapped across 15 states.** First station open in Ontario, California; first Pilot truck stop locations expected by summer 2026. The Semi supports 1.2-MW charging, restoring 60% range in ~30 minutes.
- **"Tesla Semi as a Service" model to be unveiled at ACT Expo, May 4, 2026.** Alyath plans a bundled monthly payment covering vehicle, charging infrastructure, and energy — eliminating fleet capex barriers.
- **Model Y L unveiled in India; deliveries starting this summer.** Model Y L Premium AWD priced at ₹61,99,000 (~$66,600 USD), approximately 9% cheaper than the smaller Model Y Premium RWD in that market.
- **NHTSA closes Model Y steering wheel probe without action.** The preliminary evaluation covering 120,089 2023 Model Y vehicles regarding steering wheel detachment reports was formally closed with no action against Tesla.

## Financials
- **Q1 2026 beat across revenue, gross margin, EPS, and free cash flow.** Bhakdi described auto margins as "positively surprised" — unexpected upside. CIC noted midpoint gross margins showed continued improvement.
- **2026 capex guidance raised $5B to $25B total.** Institutional analysts broadly framed the increase as a growth investment, not a negative. Roth Capital's Craig Irwin explicitly called it a positive and redirected attention to long-term growth including the Terafab facility.
- **Institutional price targets post-earnings: $465–$550.** Cantor Fitzgerald $510 (overweight), CIC $500 (outperform), Baird $522 (lowered from $538, outperform maintained), RBC $465 (buy), Roth Capital ~$550 (buy). No major downgrades.
- **Tesla converted its $2B xAI investment into a direct SpaceX equity stake.** Bloomberg reported the conversion on March 12, 2026, ahead of SpaceX's planned IPO. This is a structural balance sheet shift, not a routine financial transaction.

## Market & Competition
- **SpaceX IPO reportedly being roadshowed at $1.75T valuation, raising $75B, June 2026 target.** Bhakdi and others discuss a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger mechanism post-IPO. Chamath Palihapitiya stated he is "99% sure" a reverse merger will happen. K2 Merger Sub Inc. and K2 Merger Sub 2 LLC were filed in Nevada on January 21, 2026.
- **Xpeng identified as only credible global challenger to Tesla in autonomy.** Genma notes Xpeng went full vision-only, end-to-end from scratch after FSD V12 in July 2024, built its own Turing chip (3,000 TOPS, 200,000+ cumulative units shipped), and is offering VLA 2.0 free to all Turing-equipped owners. Projected ~500,000 vehicles running VLA 2.0 by end of 2026. Remaining gaps vs. Tesla: ~30,000 GPUs (roughly 5x less compute than Cortex) and no Turing chip in training loop. Genma predicts Xpeng unsupervised release in 2028.
- **Legacy OEM catch-up blocked by politics, not technology.** Genma argues a competent team could have a drivable FSD mule in 9–12 months and production intent in 24–36 months — but internal politics (ADAS team redundancies, supplier contract clauses, executive ego) make adoption structurally unlikely. Elon stated he offered FSD licensing to legacy OEMs and they declined.
- **U.S. gas prices at multi-year high: $4.18/gallon nationally, ~$6 in California.** Model Y Premium operating cost ~$0.04/mile vs. $0.104/mile for a Toyota RAV4 Hybrid — a 61% cost-per-mile advantage, structurally strengthening the EV demand case.

Notable quotes and data:
- Genma: *"The HD map is not a feature. It is proof that the intelligence is missing."*
- Genma: *"The rocket is about to launch. The others are going to be left in the mud."*
- Bhakdi: *"I believe we have already passed the Rubicon. We kind of have already passed the inflection point."*
- Elon at 2025 shareholders meeting: *"You actually have to train for integer inference — which everyone else is training for floating point."*
- Active Robotaxi fleet: **649** (RobotaxiTracker.com, April 30); unsupervised subset: **25**
- Cybercab production rate: **~300/month** (Bhakdi); year-end target: **10,000–20,000** deployed
- Q1 2026 capex guidance: **$25B** total (raised $5B)
- Institutional price targets: **$465–$550**
- Tesla Semi: **965 of 1,067** California Clean Truck voucher applications (Jan 2025–Feb 2026)
- HW3 collective claim: **~3,000 owners, 29 countries, €6.5M**
- Cortex: **~40,000 AI4 chips + ~90,000 H100 GPUs**, built for **~$2B**; AWS equivalent: **$5.5–$6B/year**
- Cybercab: **~$25,000–$30,000** production cost; **~4,000 parts**; **500K–1M mile** target lifespan
